## Chapter XII. On the Effects of Good and Bad Conscience

*De Effectibus Bonae et Malae Conscientiae.*

Beyond what has already been said of the seared conscience — those inured through custom to whoremongers, gamblers, litigators, embezzlers, guileful contractors in their dealings, and the like, than which nothing is more common in the world; who indeed sin with impunity, yet in the heart still feel their own torment. For every voluntary transgression of law that comes with delight, however it may be palliated before the world, still *wounds the conscience* — one must observe the following effects.

**Firstly, tranquillity and gladness of heart signify a good conscience; anxiety, fear, and sadness a bad one.** For these are the proper effects of conscience, as we have said above. And though the pious also sometimes grieve and fear, they grieve not because of their own guilt but on account of some outward and common evils that afflict even the strongest — meanwhile placing their inward trust in the Lord, tranquil in the very midst of the world's waves. Because *if our heart condemn us not, we have confidence toward God* (1 John 3:21). So also the impious sometimes bear before themselves a certain gladness or high-spiritedness — but it is a false pretext and mere show; for it lacks the true foundation, the tranquillity of the heart, since *he who is evilly conscious always presumes evil things* (Wisd 17:11): *there is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked* (Isa 57:21).

**Secondly**, when a man is not conscious of any grave crime, and does not feel himself inclined toward one, but abhors it and detests those who commit such things, he enjoys a good conscience — though at times, on account of lukewarmness in prayers and love of God, he is more fearful. For such fear is filial and can coexist with — nay, preserves — good conscience. Solomon (Prov 28:14): *Happy is the man that feareth alway.* And on the opposite side (Ps 2:11): *Serve the Lord with fear.* So Job says: *I was afraid of all my works* (Job 9:28); and yet elsewhere: *my heart shall not reproach me any of my days* (Job 27:6) — which was the testimony of a good conscience.

**Thirdly**, if a man has sinned most gravely, yet has done penance, and does not rejoice in the recollection of past sin but abominates it, he has a good conscience — for what was formerly polluted by sin is now, through the blood of Christ, cleansed *from dead works* (Heb 9:14). Hence John writes: *If our heart reprove us, God is greater than our heart* (1 John 3:20).

**Fourthly**, whoever fears God and loves his Word, prays diligently, willingly serves his neighbor, keeps himself from his own harms, bears injuries patiently, guards himself from sins, grieves over the law of sin in his members, and mourns that he cannot in all things perfectly observe God's commandments — yet with his utmost strength strives to serve God, and prays that God may succor his weakness — he has no cause to doubt of his good conscience. For all these are works of the Spirit of God, *who will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins* (Wisd 1:4).

**Fifthly** — as we shall see when treating the healing of a wounded conscience — even a mind once grievously wounded may be brought back to good conscience by the ministry of the Word and the application of Christ's satisfaction.

**Sixthly**, a good conscience delights in the fellowship of Christ through the participation of his Body and Blood in the Holy Eucharist. *Christ dwells in our hearts by faith* (Eph 3:17); more intimately still he unites himself to us through the communication of his Body and Blood (John 6:56 f.).

— ❦ —

## Chapter XIII. Why Christians Especially Should Take Account of Conscience

*Quod Christianis imprimis Conscientia rationem sit.*

The devil's malice contrives to remove from the eyes of many the very care of conscience. Therefore we must set down four reasons that should stir every man to the study of a good conscience.

**First, on account of God**, who commands us the purity of conscience, and demands of us a life without stain in his Word. Hence the summary of the mandate is called *charity out of a pure heart, of a good conscience, and of faith unfeigned* (1 Tim 1:5). Hence Solomon (Prov 4:23): *Keep thy heart with all diligence, for out of it are the issues of life.* Hence Christ's mandate that *our light so shine before men, that they may see our good works, and glorify our Father which is in heaven* (Matt 5:16). And Paul: *that thou keep this commandment without spot, unrebukable, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ* (1 Tim 6:14).

**Second, on account of the holy angels**, who are exhilarated by the pious and holy works of men, but grieved by impure and evil ones (Rev 12:10). Whose office we cannot better sustain than by studying to guard an unspotted conscience. It is worth the labor, therefore, that each man take account of all the paths of his life, accuse himself, and free his conscience. *Anticipate thy accuser: if thou wilt accuse thyself, thou shalt not fear thy accuser* — so Ambrose (*De poenitentia* ii, c. 7).

**Third, on account of the devil** — so that we may give him no occasion to accuse us. For our *accuser stands before God day and night* (Rev 12:10). So that we may fear no evil, since the pain of a lost conscience carries with it the loss of God's favor, the sorrow of the angels, the fear of death, the accusation of the devil, the gnawing of conscience, and the terror of hell.

**Fourth, and chiefly, on account of ourselves.** For with a good conscience lost, all our felicity perishes; with it kept, our highest good is retained. Hence the verse: *If you lose all things, remember to guard your good name — for once lost, it will belong to no one after.* This must be considered a little more carefully.

*First*, with a good conscience is lost at the same time **faith**, and all the gifts that in faith are divinely bestowed upon us. For in Christians, faith and good conscience cohere by an indissoluble bond, so that the one cannot be retained without the other. Wherefore Paul in summing up the mandate names *faith unfeigned, conscience good* (1 Tim 1:5, 19), and joins these two — establishing that when good conscience is repelled, faith suffers shipwreck. So he bids the minister of the Church *hold the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience* (1 Tim 3:9). *Who having put away this*, he says, *concerning faith have made shipwreck* (1 Tim 1:19). And unbelievers are said also to have *defiled conscience* (Titus 1:15). So faith and complete good conscience are conjoined (Heb 10). When therefore good conscience is lost, faith too is lost; and so it follows that whoever does not have good conscience is *not in grace with God* — since *without faith it is impossible to please God* (Heb 11:6). Hence Paul joins good conscience with the grace of God (1 Cor 1:2).

Thereby we lose the **remission of sins**, which by faith in Christ we receive (Acts 10:43); for the blood of Christ purges the conscience from dead works, that we may serve the living God (Heb 9:14). We lose the **righteousness before God** which is by faith, as all Scripture testifies; the **access to God with confidence** which is ascribed to faith (Rom 5:1) and to a good conscience (1 John 3:21); the **indwelling of Christ and of the Holy Spirit** in us — for such indwelling belongs to those *who keep the word of Christ* (John 14:23). Finally, we lose **the hope of eternal life** — into which nothing unclean shall enter (Rev 21:27). Whence of the impious it is read at the last day (Wisd 4:20): *In the reckoning of their sins they shall come with fear, and their iniquities shall convict them face to face.* It is therefore of the utmost concern that each man strive to keep his conscience unspotted. For *what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?* (Matt 16:26).

*Then*, with a good conscience are lost **all the exercises of true faith**. Prayers perish — being lukewarm, or plainly none, or at least without fruit. For they are done without faith, by those who sin mortally; and *God hears not sinners* (John 9:31). So God turned aside the prayers even of those who prayed with an evil conscience (Isa 1:15). Whereto Paul: he wills that we lift up *holy hands*, without wrath and doubting (1 Tim 2:8). Alms perish also, because they are done without the sufficient direction of conscience; and all other works of mercy — vigils, labors, and countless duties — no matter how diligently performed, because without faith and good conscience they are done, either of custom, of example, or of necessity — never with acquiescence in these things themselves.

*Thirdly*, with good conscience lost, **all consolation and courage in adversity** are lost. For a good conscience is fitting refreshment to a regenerate mind; it despises the threats of enemies, and not only lifts the cross but even makes it sweet, and blunts the assault of temptations even in the very agony of death — of which all are destitute who have not a good conscience.

*Fourthly*, with good conscience is lost **the tranquillity of life**. For good conscience is the joyful state of the whole life — but especially the sweet nurse of old age. Wherefore Samuel, already gray, appeals in the presence of the whole people to the innocence of his life (1 Sam 12:2 ff.). And an old man, asked by a young one why his old age was so pleasant, replied: *A free youth was my youth.* An evil conscience, however, is like a butcher or a most savage beast, gaping after the life and blood of the man even in this most fortunate world — bringing on perpetual fear and horror.

*Fifthly*, with good conscience lost is lost the **hope of a blessed death**. For they die evil who have lived evilly — and a corrupt conscience prepares a precipice to despair, especially when again and again it is agitated. It is folly to think, as many do, that upon perceiving they have sinned they can then fly to God's mercy. For many sins have so lulled the man to sleep that he never comes to serious recognition of sin: their conscience itself is so twisted by such tortures that they cannot seriously think of the mercy of God, whence they rush headlong into the abyss of despair — either becoming numb in themselves and dying as beasts (like *Nabal* in 1 Sam 25) or laying violent hands upon themselves (like *Cain, Saul, Ahithophel, Judas*). Since this is so, it is worth-while indeed to preserve conscience without a stain — which should be the chief care of all the faithful. Hence Bernard's saying:

*Hodie sit mea prima cura, ut te quaeram mente pura.*
*(Today let this be my first care, that with pure mind I seek thee.)*

— ❦ —

## Chapter XIV. How Conscience is Healed, if it has been Wounded

*Quomodo Sanetur Conscientia, si forte Vulnerata Fuerit.*

Conscience is wounded by actions disagreeing with law, through headlong falls that sometimes overtake even the regenerate. For the falls of the regenerate are twofold: some *of infirmity*, done unwillingly; others *of malice*, done with set purpose and against conscience — and these last shake off grace and faith. In these, when conscience resists yet is not restrained, conscience is said to be *wounded*.

**When conscience is thus wounded, there is no other remedy but this: that the wound be cured by that same blood of Christ which cleanses our conscience from dead works (Heb 9:14).** For Christ is the immaculate Lamb of God, who offered himself as a sacrifice for our sins (1 Pet 1:19); and as he took our sins upon himself, so also his conscience, laden with alien guilt, was made most sorrowful. So that all his agonies bear witness to that time; on which account *his soul was sorrowful even unto death* (Matt 26:38); and with his prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears he sufficiently expressed to God the anguish and press of his soul (Heb 5:7) — anguish which he suffered not for his own merit but for the guilt of others.

Therefore this alone is the sufficient remedy for the healing of our wounded consciences; and since in the very agony it did not fail — being not human but divine — it is therefore now to be applied to the wounded conscience.

**The application is by the ministry of the Word**, in which is required (from the minister's part) preaching of Law and of Gospel. By the *Law* the wound is displayed and pain is stirred, without which sense of pain no cure is possible; then by the *Gospel* the grace of God is announced through Christ, who cries to all truly penitent: *Come unto me, all ye that labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest* (Matt 11:28). *For if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins* (1 John 1:9). *Whosesoever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them* (John 20:23) — the classical scriptural form of absolution, entrusted to Christ's ministers.

Yet on the sinner's part is required *contrition*, *confession*, and *faith* — the same threefold operation of true penance so familiar in Wittenberg dogmatics.

- **Contrition** arises from the acknowledgment of sin, which extorts sorrow and anguish of conscience, so that the man judges himself unworthy of any mercy.
- **Confession** is the acknowledgment of sin — first before *God*, who alone has the power of remitting sins, David's example (Ps 32:5, Ps 51); and then before that *neighbor whom we have offended* (which other confession is called *reconciliation*, Matt 5:23 f.), and *before the minister of the Word* (James 5:16), from whom absolution is heard.
- **Faith** consists not merely in a *notice* of Christ's merits — for even the devils believe (James 2:19) — nor merely in *assent* to what Scripture declares of Christ; but chiefly in the applying to oneself in individual assurance of what Christ has done for all. Whence he can say: *Christ loved me, and gave himself for me* (Gal 2:20). This confidence sets up the man's stricken mind, and holds him back from the precipice of despair, so that concerning the reconciliation with an offended God he promises himself the best things through Christ, whose wrath being appeased, the conscience is also pacified — and the man is excused, absolved from condemnation, because his sins have already been laid on Another, by whom abundant satisfaction has been made for them. To this the Spirit of God (*who intercedes for us with groanings which cannot be uttered*) bears witness — *the Spirit himself beareth witness with our spirit that we are the children of God* (Rom 8:16).

So at length the anguishes of the heart vanish, gladness returns in the Lord, and the conscience, which was before like a hell, is converted into a most joyful paradise.

— ❦ —

## Chapter XV. Whether Conscience Can Be Extinguished in a Man

*An Conscientia in Homine Extingui Possit.*

**Conscience, being a natural light in man, cannot utterly be extinguished** — though it is often for a season *impeded* from its office, so that it does not judge rightly of the actions of men, nor accuse them. When this happens, it seems as it were extinguished and buried.

Conscience is impeded in its office in various ways:

**1.** *Externally*, when some cause obscures the judgment of honest and base actions, so that they are not recognized — as in *frenetics and maniacs*, who commit homicide or similar without murmur of conscience, because they do not understand what they are doing.

**2.** *By the outward force of the affections*, which as by a dense fog obscures the mind so that it cannot recognize what it does; when that fog is repelled, it understands rightly, and conscience awakens as from the depths. An example is in the *angered*: *the fury of anger is brief; while it operates, one is not sane before God* (James 1:20). For the heat of anger disturbs the mind, so that while the man commits murder he thinks he does right, until his heat abates — then he first feels the sting of conscience. Cain provides the example. So the *lustful* is captivated when the flesh sweetly stirs him, and does not feel any bite or reluctance of conscience in the very act — but afterward, once done, he perceives the wound.

**3.** *By the will's decision* not to allow conscience any voice in an impious deed. As appears in those who persecute confessors of the heavenly doctrine under the name of heretics: of whom Christ warned (John 16:2): *The time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service* — *and this they will do to you, because they have not known the Father, nor me.*

**4.** *By hardness of obstination* — for conscience sleeps not as a watchman, but as a wild beast that has ceased its roar or as a hoarse dog: in some it is so lulled by the sluggishness of sin that in all the time of life no bark or spur is felt from it. Nevertheless, it will awake at least in death, when it flogs the man at a most untimely hour.

Such consciences are either always impeded in their office, or only for a time. *Always impeded* — when men are given over to a *reprobate mind* (Rom 1:28), so that they judge good to be evil and evil to be good, and thus in erring judgment persist and perish without repentance. Thus many, on account of heresy or some horrid crime, endure the bitterest torments without any prick of conscience — as Faustus's example and those who slew kings whom they held to be heretics testify. Not always impeded, in those who at length by the sense of divine punishments, or by the exhortations of the pious, wake themselves up — as *Joseph's brethren* did (Gen 37, 42), who did not immediately, upon selling their brother, acknowledge how great a crime they had done — but ate their bread securely; and when treated more harshly in Egypt, they felt the anguishes of their former crime: *We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear* (Gen 42:21).

Such conscience is called **dormant** (not extinct — for it is not utterly dead). It *sleeps* in a restless bed, ever able to be awakened; yet though it always murmurs and accuses, it never spurs unto good (as in the damned).

Therefore let us admit betimes those means by which we can shake off the torpor of conscience. For it is better that we be afflicted in the time of grace than that we perish in the time of wrath. There the anguishes of conscience can carry their *sadness that worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of* (2 Cor 7:10). But here in many, whose repentance death cuts short, they become the beginning of infernal torments.

— ❦ —

## Chapter XVI. What a Case of Conscience is, and How Many Kinds

*Quid sit Casus Conscientiae et Quotuplex.*

*Case* takes its name from *falling* (*cadendo*). In grammar it is the same as *lapse* or *ruin*. In *physics* it is a cause per accidens of things that come to pass beyond choice for the sake of some end. In *ethics* it is a fall or some vice or exorbitance from the middle. In the same manner it is used in **theology**: whence the saying — *A holy man walks in his fall of conscience, because he is headlong into vice.*

Some call a *case of conscience* any action departing from right reason and repugnant to it; more correctly, however, it is called a *scruple* or *doubt* in some action of a man, concerning which conscience cannot without information carry out its own judgment under a certain determination. Whatever befalls a man in which his judgment can err, is called a case of conscience — which, so long as it is directed by right judgment, keeps conscience good; but when it errs, it is a fall and wounds the conscience.

Hence *case of conscience*, of *lapses* or actions departing from right reason. In this signification is distinguished, in the papacy, between **reserved cases** and **non-reserved cases**.

*A reserved case is that whose absolution is forbidden to an inferior priest.* It is either **papal** (whose absolution belongs solely to the Pope, and forbidden to bishops and pastors) or **episcopal** (whose absolution is granted to the bishop only, and forbidden to pastors). On this see the Council of Trent (Sess. 14, c. 7), Chemnitz (*Loci Theologici*, s.v. *Clavium*), and Tolet (*Instructionis Sacerdotum* Book 3).

**But this distinction is completely without foundation, and has been thought up for the establishing of the Pope's absolute power.** For absolution from sins is not to be governed by human arbitration; and where the ministry of the sacred office is exercised — the remission of sins is announced without accepting persons who minister thereto. For this power is no greater in the Roman Pontifex than in the humblest deacon, since it is *ministerial in all and apostolic, exercised by God's dispensation for our stewardship*.

Yet if by *reason* they are joined for Christ (2 Cor 5:20), they are judges of consciences but not dispensers — they are stewards of the remission of sins, not authors and lords. Even so, this reservation of cases does not pertain to us.

**A case of conscience, in the wider sense of which we speak, pertains to the actions of men considered with respect to their propriety** — to which action must be tempered and shaped, so that it agree with right reason. And these questions branch over the whole life of man in its several kinds.

**Cases of conscience are divided variously by various authors.**

- Some divide them *according to the offices of the priest*, as does **Francisco de Toledo**.
- Some divide them *according to the considerations of the man*, whether *simply in himself* or *with respect to God and neighbor*. The former yields questions of what the man must do, how he may be received into the grace of God and preserved therein, how he may be certain of his salvation, how he may collect himself when troubled in mind. The latter yields questions of *the worship of God* and of the actions of man as he is a member of the Church, family, or commonwealth. This is the order followed by **Guilielmus Perkinsius** (William Perkins).
- Others distribute them *according to the parts of the catechetical doctrine* — placing cases about the several precepts of the Decalogue, about the several articles of the Creed, about the petitions of the Lord's Prayer, and about each of the Sacraments. This order is observed by **Hemmingius** (Niels Hemmingsen).

**In this treatise, however, since the method is free to any writer, we shall distribute the cases of conscience *according to the object of the man's action*.** For man's action is either:

- *In matters divine and concerning religion* — that is, toward *God* (Book II).
- *Turned toward angels and spirits* — celestial spirits, angels, demons, astrology, magic (Book III).
- *Occupied with human things* — either the state of body and fortune, or the salvation of the soul (Book IV, part 1).
- *Directed toward the neighbor* — in ecclesiastical, political, and economic condition (Book IV, part 2).

By this order we shall now set about the decisions of the cases of conscience, imploring the grace and blessing of God with our humble voices.

— ❦ —

## Additamentum — Two Questions from the *Table of Good and Bad Conscience* of D. Johann Steuber

*Additamentum ad Librum hunc Primum, sumptum ex D. Joh. Steuberi Conscientiae Boni et Malae Tabula.*

*(Editor's note: two supplementary questions appended by the widow-heirs in the 1628 edition, drawn from the tabular casuistical apparatus of Johann Steuber — an early-17th-century Wittenberg-Marburg Lutheran casuist. They pick up the same practical questions Balduin has been asking, in the tabular scholastic key.)*

### Quaestio I. How is Good Conscience to be Preserved?

The preservation of good conscience is most necessary — since *whatever is not of faith is sin* (Rom 14:23). Paul commends the retention of good conscience to Timothy: *This charge I commit unto thee, son Timothy, according to the prophecies which went before on thee, that thou by them mightest war a good warfare; holding faith, and a good conscience; which some having put away concerning faith have made shipwreck* (1 Tim 1:18–19).

Great is the force of conscience on either side: that they are not afraid who have not sinned, and they perpetually think the punishment set before their eyes who have sinned (Cicero, *Pro Milone*). *Conscia mens ut cuique sua est, ita concipit intra pectora pro facto spemque metumque suo* (Ovid, *Fasti* i). *Whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme* (1 Tim 1:20). Conscience keeps mendacities as its whip; the mind is *tortor* to itself when guilty. So none — not even those who deny that we can wholly fall from justifying faith by reigning sins — can flatter themselves in the depravity of this dictum.

**By what means is an untainted conscience to be preserved?** By five ordered means:

**1. Attentive meditation on the divine majesty and accurate consideration of the divine Word by which God speaks to us in Sacred Scripture.** Because we are all sinners, our conscience is stained — therefore it must be purged by the application of the purification acquired by the blood of Christ (1 John 1:7), obtained through faith. Thus purified, our conscience must study new obedience according to the law of God, and shun the vices that would defile conscience — considering that saying of Sirach (13:30): *There is no wealth above health of body: and no joy above the joy of heart.*

**2. Devoted colloquy with God** — a humble address of God (Cyprian, *Ep.* 1) in the name of Christ, that he may clothe us with the Holy Spirit (Luke 11:13), who leads us in the level path (Ps 143:10). *The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much* (James 5:16).

**3. Intimate association with Christ through the participation of his Body and Blood in the Holy Eucharist.** Christ indeed dwells in our hearts by faith (Eph 3:17); but more intimately still he unites himself to us through communication of his Body and Blood (John 6:56). To eat his flesh and drink his blood spiritually (which spiritual eating and drinking is required for the saving use of the Holy Supper) is to abide in him, and he in us — and he who abides in him will bear much fruit; for without him we can do nothing (John 15:5). Effectually the Word of God gives us life (Heb 4:12); the Body and Blood of Christ (John 6:55, 6:53–54) — when the former is given for us, and the latter poured out for us for the remission of our sins (Luke 22:19–20; Matt 26:28; Mark 14:24). The Word of God makes us certain in general of the remission of sins and confirms our faith; but the Holy Eucharist exhibits to us, by means of bread and wine, the Body and Blood of Christ as a pledge of redemption — and announces to each of us individually that the Body of Christ was given into death for me who eats the blessed bread, and his Blood was shed for me who drinks the blessed cup, for the remission of the sins that I have committed.

**4. Daily reflection on some incitements to piety.** Many such exercises of piety abound; among the eminent are:

- **To think of God as present in every action.** Tobit commended it to his son (Tob 4:5): *All thy days keep the Lord God our God in mind; and beware, lest by doing contrary to his commandments, thou sin.* Solomon (Prov 3:6): *In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.* David (Ps 16:8): *I have set the Lord always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.* Who would in the sight of husband, father, teacher, master, or even judge commit some heinous crime? But God is everywhere present (Sir 24:8 ff.); nor can man hide himself in darkness from him (Wisd 17:2). His eyes are a thousand times brighter than the sun; they behold all the ways of men, the depths, and the concealed parts of the heart (Sir 23:28). *He is our Father* (Isa 63:16), *our Lord* (Luke 6:46), *our benefactor* (Acts 14:17, 17:25), whom villainy displeases (Prov 6:5), *the judge of the living and the dead* (Acts 10:42), who *will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will manifest the counsels of the hearts* (1 Cor 4:5). Therefore keep continually before thyself the three things: *his Eye*, which sees all our thoughts, words, and deeds, even in the hidden parts (Sir 23); *his Ear*, which attends to all our thoughts, words, and deeds (Ps 94:8–10); *his Book*, in which are inscribed all our thoughts, words, and deeds, that from it we may be judged on the last day (Rev 20:12).

- **To keep in memory the Four Last Things** — *death, extreme judgment, eternal life, infernal pain* — as Sirach urges (Sir 7): *In all thy negotiations, remember thy last end, and thou shalt never sin.*

    - *In recalling death, four things are to be considered*: (i) the *certitude* of death (Ps 89:48; Heb 9:27); (ii) the *uncertainty of its time*, kind, and our own constitution — we know not on what day, hour, or moment, nor in what place, we shall be seized (Prov 27:1); (iii) the *danger* — *if the tree fall toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falleth, there it shall be* (Eccl 11:3); (iv) the *leaving-behind of riches, honors, pleasures* and all worldly goods, which if I ponder as things to be relinquished at death, I shall not be offended when I see the impious rich, nor covet their honors and delights.

    - *The memory of the extreme judgment is fivefold and to be dreaded*: (i) the *citation to judgment* by the sound of the trumpet (1 Cor 15:52; 1 Thess 4:16); (ii) the *strict examination* of all thoughts, words, and works of the heart, even *for every idle word* (Matt 12:36) and every doubtful thing, every stewardship of goods; (iii) the *Judge* — Christ Jesus, judge of quick and dead (John 5:22; Acts 10:42), supreme (Matt 25:32), strong and almighty (Ps 45:3–4), inflexible (Acts 10:42; James 1:17), omniscient (Heb 4:13), just (Rom 2:5–11), angry (Ps 76:3); (iv) the *accusers and witnesses* — a multitude will come forth: conscience (Rom 2:15), fellow-sinners (Wisd 5:3–8), doctors and teachers (Heb 13:17; John 12:48), just and holy men (Wisd 4:16), the devil (Rev 12:10), all creatures (Rom 8:19–22); (v) the *definitive sentence upon the impious*: *depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels* — a sentence which comprehends everlasting separation from God, from the holy angels, from all the elect — *everlasting malediction*, *everlasting fire*, *everlasting, sad, and horrid cohabitation with devils*, and *irrevocable committal to infernal pains*.

    - *In the contemplation of eternal life* is represented: the insatiable *vision of the divine Majesty* (Matt 5:8; Job 19:26; 1 Cor 13:12; 1 John 3:2); the ineffable *condition of eternal life* (1 Cor 2:9; Ps 16:11); the *continual glorification of God* (Rev 4:8, 7:11 f.); the *soul's adornment* — intellect elevated in wisdom (1 Cor 2:9–10), will in sanctity (Matt 5:8), affections conformed to the will of God (Eph 5:17); the *body's clarity*, conformed to Christ's body (Phil 3:21) and to the angels (Matt 22:30; Luke 20:36), in clarity (Wisd 3:7; Dan 12:3; Matt 13:43), swiftness (1 Thess 4:17), strength (1 Cor 15:44), invisibility (Luke 24:31), immortality (1 Cor 15:52–53; Rev 21:4), power for penetration, restored vigor of powers (Isa 40:31), perfection of nature not subject to reparation by food or drink (Isa 49:10; Rev 7:16); the *pleasant fellowship and converse with Christ* (John 12:26; John 14:3; 1 Thess 4:17), with the holy angels (Heb 12:22), and with all the elect (Matt 8:11; Luke 13:28; Heb 12:23).

    - *In pondering infernal pain*, terror will strike us: *everlasting separation* from God, from angels, from the elect (Matt 7:23; Matt 13:41–42; Matt 25:41; Luke 13:27–28; Luke 17:34–36); *horrid fellowship with the very devils themselves* (Matt 25:41); *extreme* pain (Job 6:15), *continual* (Rev 20:10), *infinite* (Rev 14:11; 19:3), of torture and torment; *extreme darkness* (Matt 8:12; 13:42; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30; Luke 13:28); *inextinguishable fire* (Isa 66:24; Mark 9:44; Matt 13:42, 25:41); *unsupportable thirst* (Zech 14:6; Matt 8:12; Luke 16:24); *vapor and sulphurous stench* (Isa 34:9–10; Rev 14:10, 19:19, 20:14, 21:8); *gnawing conscience* (Isa 66:24); the *sense of divine wrath* (Wisd 12:10; Matt 3:7; John 3:36; 1 Thess 1:10; Rev 6:16–17); *perpetual death* (Ps 49:14; Rev 2:11, 20:6, 20:14, 21:8); *hunger and thirst* (Isa 65:13; Rev 18:8; Luke 16:24).

**5. Strict moderation of thoughts, words, members, and the whole body.** Our thoughts are either good, evil, or indifferent. *Good* — those to be tenaciously held to, praying God that he render us fit to think anything good (2 Cor 3:5) and that he make us both will and do (Phil 2:13). *Evil* — as soon as they arise, to be strangled and inhibited, lest they provoke delight; delight, consent; consent, act; act, custom; custom, habit; and habit, a seared conscience. *Indifferent* — pleasing to God if directed to a good end according to God's Word, in due place and time; otherwise displeasing.

*In speech*, that no man offend and that no man's tongue destroy him, one must set a guard over the mouth (Sir 22:33) — that speech be silent, when it is not provoked to colloquy, when office nor station requires it. *He is wise who is discovered in silence, when opportunity would offer speech; and he is silent because he has nothing to answer* (Sir 20). *A silent tongue is a token of a wise soul* (Sir 22:33). But when necessity of speaking is laid on us, then before speech we must first weigh (a) *the truth* of what we say — for lying is condemned (Prov 12:22); (b) the *right time* and (c) the *usefulness* of what is said, in due measure — lest it obscure the good things spoken.

*Concerning the members* — one is to guard them from every evil and appearance of evil (1 Thess 5:22). Paul calls this a *crucifying of the flesh with its affections and lusts* (Gal 5:24), a *crucifying of the old man*, an *abolition of the body of sin* (Rom 6:6), a *mortification of the deeds of the flesh through the Spirit* (Rom 8:13), a *putting to death of the members which are upon the earth* (Col 3:5), a *putting off of the old man and putting on of the new* (Eph 4:22 ff.; Col 3:9–10). To which end contribute much: sobriety and moderation of food and drink, so that the body may not be poured out to luxury.

**Truly, none but with a good conscience is loosed** — which, if we would fully consider, would abominate falling. *Look upward*: man deserts God, and exposes himself to the devil's power. *Look downward*: horrible it is that a man should so forget himself as to send God's messenger away — that same God who created him from the mud, restored him by his Word, freed him from every evil, gave him life through the entire span of his days (Gen 48; Ps 27:15). *Look about*: he pours out all creatures for himself, and makes all the members of the human body witnesses of his kindnesses. Look horrible! that a man should destroy God so malignantly, when he alone is the supreme and immense good. Whence *sin* — which separates from God — is called *the greatest evil*. Look forward: sin is unworthy of a Christian (Phil 1:27), and beyond the reign of heaven.

Set before thee the example of Joseph (Gen 39): *conscience-taught*, he despised his mistress's foul demand, cared not for prison or ill fame. Set before thee Susanna, who preferred to perish innocently than to sin against her conscience by adultery (Hist. Susanna 22–23). Set before thee the Apostles, who went forth from the Council of the Priests rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer disgrace for his name — nor could they be bent by threats or scourging to obey men more than God (Acts 5:41).

### Quaestio II. Whether Reputation Can Sometimes Take Priority Over Conscience

There are twin things: **conscience** and **reputation**. *Conscience is necessary to thyself; reputation is necessary to thy neighbor: whoso trusts to his own conscience but neglects his reputation is cruel* (Augustine, *Ad fratres in eremo*, sermon 32). Reputation must be preserved on account of ourselves most wisely; on account of others most mercifully. Augustine again (*Sermon 46, de diversis*): *They are not to be heard, whether men or women, who when they are rebuked in some negligence, lest they come into evil suspicion (whence they know their life is far removed), say that before God their conscience suffices, and yet contemptuously — indeed cruelly — despise the estimation of men. They slay the souls of others, either of the blasphemers of the way of God, who by suspicion (as if base) suspect the chaste and pleasing life of the saints, or even of those who imitate what they do not see but what they think.* Therefore *whoever guards his life against the outrages of profligacies and crimes does well by himself; whoever also his good name is merciful to others. Our life is necessary to us, our reputation to others.* Augustine, *De bono viduitatis* c. 11: *They are not to be heard.*

**Yet reputation is never to be redeemed at the cost of a good conscience.** The *order of charity* must be observed — as to the person to be loved, and as to the thing which is loved or desired in her.

*Concerning the person*, four things are to be loved out of charity:
- *First*, God, who is above us — to be loved above all things, with all the heart, soul, and strength (Deut 6:5; Matt 22:37; Rom 13:9).
- *Second*, ourselves — *for who is evil to himself, to whom shall he be good?* (Sir 14:5).
- *Third*, our neighbor, who is beside us — *Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself* (Lev 19:18; Matt 22:39).
- *Fourth*, the body of man, which is below us (Augustine, *De doctrina Christiana* i, c. 16–17; Biel, *Sent.* iii, dist. 28).

*Concerning the thing*, there are three kinds of goods that we can either desire for ourselves or for others:
- **Spiritual goods** — faith, the grace of God, good conscience, etc. — for the soul is more worthy than the body, and by natural dignity claims to itself the first solicitude (Bernard, *De adventu*, sermon 6).
- **Bodily goods** — life, health (Sir 30:15–16).
- **External goods** — reputation, honor, riches (Sir 41:15; Eccles 30:16). *This is the banner of the order of charity* (Cant 2:4).

Joining the order of charity with respect to person and to thing, each man should:
1. Love God;
2. Love himself in spiritual goods;
3. Love his neighbor in spiritual goods;
4. Love himself in bodily goods;
5. Love his neighbor in bodily goods;
6. Love himself and then his neighbor in external goods.

**The good of an inferior order is not to be redeemed by the loss of a good of a higher order, nor is the higher to yield to the lower.** *Conscience is much more to be attended to than reputation* (Publius Syrus). *Sometimes the multitude, that fickle and evil interpreter of good deeds, roars against a good man — if anything follows, it is not one's own conscience, which is also delighted by such things: which one exhibits, and against the rumor of reputation carries away the trophy — if it looks at the majesty of virtue in place of counting suffrages, one sentence conquers* (Seneca, *De vita beata* 6). *Whoever wills to publish his virtue, labors not for virtue but for glory. Do not will to be just beyond that thou art just; nay, however famous, be inwardly just. Now if thou art just, thou fearest not to praise God.* Then whoever, neglecting conscience, is willing at the risk of eternal condemnation to bring rumor to safety, is unworthy of a Christian (Phil 1:27) and out of the kingdom of heaven.

The example of Joseph is prime (Gen 39:7 ff.): conscience-taught, he cared nothing for prison or infamy but held his mistress's foul demand for nothing. Susanna preferred to die innocently rather than to commit adultery against her conscience (Susanna 22–23). The Apostles rejoiced when they went out of the Council of Priests, for they were counted worthy to be dishonored for his name — nor could they be bent by threats or lashings to obey men more than God (Acts 5:41).

**End of Liber I.**

# Liber II. Toward God and Religion

*De actionibus hominis circa Deum & religionem — On the actions of man toward God and religion.*

*(Editor's note on the 1628 print: physical pp. 87–98 in the source PDF are a partial earlier printing of Liber II Cap. I Casus I–VI — a signature that seems to have been re-set and re-bound, with p. 98 sweeping in the tail of Liber I's Steuber Additamentum under a stray "Lib. I" running header. The authoritative printing begins afresh on physical p. 99 with the full Cap. I text and continues past Casus VI into Casus VII and beyond. This translation follows the authoritative range from p. 99 / OCR ln 5308 onward and silently sets aside the pp. 87–98 duplicate.)*

## Chapter I. On Faith and the Knowledge of God from Scripture

*De fide et cognitione Dei in se, sed abstrahendo a Dei essentia, personis, attributis ejusque operibus — cases of conscience concerning faith and the knowledge of God, considered in himself but apart from his essence, persons, attributes, and works.*

### Case I. Whether the actions of man toward God are to be governed from Scripture alone, or also from some other source

The actions of man toward God do not concern the man merely externally — in things spoken or done — but embrace the man's internal thoughts and conceptions of God, all of which must be conformed to the Word of God, if conscience is to be kept unstained. For whatever is suspected of divergence from that Word, it is unlawful either to say or to think — for **to think most highly of God is the very beginning of piety**, as Augustine says (*De libero arbitrio* i).

Now man acts either *toward God* or *concerning God*: the former pertains to *faith and the knowledge of God*, the latter to *cult and religion*. And the knowledge of God is either *by ratio of himself* or *by ratio of his essence, persons, and attributes*; and each of these involves some doubtful matters, to which satisfaction must be given — that the anxious conscience be in that part consoled.

**Respondeo.** From this case we rightly take our beginning, as from the principle upon which all the rest depend. For unless something certain has first been established concerning this — that the Word of God alone is the norm and rule — the conscience will never rest in what is believed or spoken from Scripture concerning God and divine things. Ever the mind would return: *Am I sure that Scripture instructs me rightly, and that faith is to be given to it?*

**We say therefore: divine things are to be rightly and salvifically known from Scripture alone.** The reasons of this assertion are treated at length elsewhere; here, for the tranquilizing of conscience, we only draw the first outlines.

**1. First reason — the homogeneity of principles.** In all arts and disciplines, no better principle can be given than one *homogeneous*, native and proper to the discipline itself. So of things medical, from the principles of medicine; of jurisprudence, from the rules of law — most rightly is doctrine drawn. So also concerning God and divine things, nothing more rightly is judged than from the Word of God: for no man can better testify concerning God than God himself in his Word — of which no godly man doubts. Hence the well-known verses: *Let no one behold the Godhead apart from the Godhead; let no one wonder at the Sun apart from the Sun. And apart from God, God is not known.* And Irenaeus (*Adversus haereses* iv, c. 24): the *Word of God* is that which is contained in the Scripture of the Prophets and Apostles — whence Scripture is called *sacred*. God is he who has *placed his words in the mouth of the Prophet* (Jer 1:9), and *hath spoken by the mouth of his Prophets* (Luke 1:70; Acts 1:16, 3:18). *Holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost* (2 Pet 1:21). Who then shall not rest in the Word of God, when God himself is heard concerning what befits us to know of God?

**2. Second reason — the divine referral to the Word.** God himself, in matters divine, so binds us to his Word that he would have us admit nothing beyond it. *Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it* (Deut 4:2) — which precept the Lord so magnifies that with it he as it were seals up the biblical codex. Likewise it is written in Rev 22:18 f.: *I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book: and if any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life.* Ours it is, therefore, solidly to acquiesce in those things which God teaches concerning himself in his Word.

**3. Third reason — Christ's own referral.** In the New Testament Christ himself sends us to the Scriptures as to the ordinary and most certain witnesses of what is to be believed concerning him. *Search the Scriptures, for in them ye think ye have eternal life; and they are they which testify of me* (John 5:39). Whence more rightly can we come to know Christ than from those witnesses of him whom Christ himself commends?

**4. Fourth reason — Paul on the sufficiency of Scripture.** Paul testifies of the sacred letters that they *are able to make thee wise unto salvation* (2 Tim 3:15) — the Greek has *σοφίσαι*, "to make wise." Therefore the Scriptures suffice for divine wisdom and for the knowledge of those things wherein the salvation of men consists.

**5. Fifth reason — the Apostolic-Prophetic foundation.** The Church is said to be *built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets* (Eph 2:20). Therefore in the writings of the Apostles and Prophets is the true foundation of the knowledge of divine things. To which is added the consensus of the Fathers: *Not through others have we known the economy of our salvation, but through those by whom the Gospel came to us* — which they first preached, and afterwards, by the will of God, delivered to us in the Scriptures, that they might become the foundation and column of our faith (Irenaeus iii, c. 5). It is unlawful to say — as Ambrose writes, *De fide ad Gratianum* iv, c. 4: *We must not trust to argument, holy Emperor, nor to our disputation. Let us interrogate the Scriptures — let us interrogate the Apostles, let us interrogate the Prophets, let us interrogate Christ. Why should we make much of the Father? whose honor is in the same throne with him.*

Let these things suffice for the godly and studious of truth: for no other tranquility of conscience in matters of faith can there be, than what is drawn from the sacred Scriptures. What the enemies of the Scriptures, the Papists, allege concerning the imperfection and obscurity of sacred Scripture, and concerning private judgment in interpretation, has been sufficiently discussed elsewhere. Ours is not to linger here upon them, nor should the tempted commit themselves to this sea of disputations. When they see adversaries disputing against Scripture — that is, against the mouth of the Lord — they should despise that devil and consider what Irenaeus wrote (iii, c. 2): *Heretics, when they are convicted from the Scriptures, turn to accusations of the Scriptures themselves, as if they were not rightly held.*

### Case II. What if someone doubts whether he should rather believe the Scripture, or its ancient and later interpreters, whose labor many simpler folk cannot understand — in which case faith would depend on the authority of men rather than of God, and would be uncertain?

**Respondeo.** Interpreters, of whatever authority they be in the Church, are not by themselves authentic; nor is Scripture believed through them, but they are believed *because of the Scriptures* — inasmuch as their interpretation is *the analogy of faith*, which is required of every interpreter of the Scriptures (Rom 12:6). For the sense of Scripture is in Scripture itself; interpreters are nothing else than ministers and doctors, who conveniently draw forth that sense. On which account Peter wrote that *no prophecy of the Scripture is of private interpretation* (2 Pet 1:20). The reason is that Scripture proceeds from the immediate revelation of God, while our understanding, through sin, is miserably obscured — therefore it has need of the illumination of the Holy Spirit, who *hath commended himself in Scripture* (1 Cor 3:5, 5:20). Hence Augustine (*On the Interpretation of Scriptures*): *neither to himself, nor to any other, holds any faith who does not say what he says, but confirms it by the authority of the Scriptures themselves.* *Let us not hear*, he says, *these things I say, these things thou sayest — but these things the Lord saith* (*De unitate Ecclesiae* c. 3). And to Jerome (Epistle 19): *I have learned to bestow that fear and honor upon those books alone of the Scriptures which are called canonical, that I most firmly believe none of the authors thereof to have erred. Other authors I so read, that however great in sanctity and doctrine they may excel, I do not therefore hold what they hold to be true, but because they were able to persuade me either through those canonical authors themselves, or by probable reasoning.* Similar things he has in Epistle 112 to Fortunatus and elsewhere.

Since these things are so, we conclude that **interpreters, however great, are in no wise to be believed in matters of faith except insofar as their interpretation consents with the perpetual tenor of Scripture.** Upon the judgment of Scripture depends the whole truth of faith, not upon the authority of men. And so what Bellarmine writes (*De verbo Dei* i, c. 9), *that Scripture cannot interpret itself*, is manifestly against Peter's assertion, who denies Scripture stands in need of private interpretation — and against Paul, who will have the interpretation of Scripture to be *analogous to the faith*; which analogy of faith is found nowhere but in Scripture itself.

### Case III. But whence can I know that the books which are called biblical — from whose authority the faith of Christians is said to depend — are from the Spirit of God, and therefore of immoveable truth?

**Respondeo.** Of the divine authority of the sacred letters no Christian ought to doubt, for these are called *disciples of Christ who continue in his Word* (John 8:31), and the sacred letters are the principle of faith and the foundation of the Church, and the godly feel their efficacy in their hearts. For *the Spirit witnesseth, because the Spirit is truth* (1 John 5:6) — that is, the doctrine of the Spirit is of immoveable verity. Hence Augustine writes (*Confessions* vi, c. 5): *They are to be blamed, not heard, if any perhaps should say, Whence do you know that these books are the ministration to the human race of the Spirit of one true and most veracious God? — for that most of all was to be believed.*

Yet even the godly sometimes fall into such thoughts, which are to be met by these criteria and testimonies by which the majesty of Scripture is recognized:

- **1. The authority of the biblical writers**, drawn from their extraordinary vocation, mission, and inflatus, and made known by miracles (as the majesty of Christ was made known by miracles — Matt 11:5; John 3:2).
- **2. The public attestation** that God himself and the mouth of the Lord has spoken — as also strengthened by the very weight of the things themselves: for they treat of divine mysteries surpassing every grasp of human reason.
- **3. The miracles by which God himself procured authority to his doctrine** — in Egypt, in the desert, and elsewhere — so that even the gentiles from them recognized *the finger of the Lord* (Exod 8:19).
- **4. The prophetic revelations, which the event answered most exactly** — which Scripture proclaims as manifestly a divine work (Isa 41:23).
- **5. The venerable sanctity of the biblical books.** Nothing base, nothing scandalous, nothing self-contradictory is found in them; and what has the appearance of such is easily reconciled — an argument which Augustine especially urges (*De utilitate credendi* c. 6).
- **6. The style — the accidental humility that breathes the efficacious virtue of divine power.** *For the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power* (1 Cor 4:20).
- **7. The admirable harmony and consonance of both Testaments** — whence the ancients said: *The New in the Old is figured; the Old in the New is fulfilled.* Plures such majestic marks see in Hunnius's excellent little book *De majestate Scripturae*.

There are those who bite at biblical books with impunity: **the gentiles**, who — even though they do not ignore that some numen exists — cannot say what it is; therefore not only did they make men to be gods, but heaven, the planets, stars, fruits, plants, herbs, shields, swords, ancilia, fear, dread, boldness, and their own other affections. And though Varro (in Augustine *De civitate Dei* iv, c. 9 and 11) reckons the gentiles to have named many gods and goddesses but comprised all in one Jupiter, whose those faculties and functions were — yet who this Jupiter might be, they were ignorant. Whence *that woman in Euripides*, invoking Jove, cried out: *O Jupiter, whosoever thou art, help me.* Of the same kind is another story of one who thus addressed the Egyptians: *If ye are gods, weep not; if dead, why do ye adore them?* — this indeed is not to have faith concerning God but opinion.

To this class belong also **those who thought only what they had seen** — declaring God to be, only because no one had ever seen him. Of whose number are they who through magic art have shown demons to be seen, and, having seen them, believed there was a God. These too conceived opinion rather than faith concerning God: whom the gentiles themselves for that reason called **Atheists**.

And there are in the Church **doctors** who, by too much disputing about God, lose all certainty and retain nothing but opinion — never satisfied with themselves; whence their faith in temptation vanishes like sparks, no solid foundation being laid; which happens to those who praise themselves also for making dubious in whatever way the Christian and scriptural doctrine about the three persons in one divine essence, or the two natures in Christ, and the like — among whom is Erasmus, and today's Photinians, who opine rather than believe of God.

By these are seduced the **simpler folk**, who, when they hear the altercations of the learned about God and divine things, begin themselves to *shake*, and merely to opine what they ought to believe — because they cannot compose such disputes. But their conscience is by that ratio never rendered tranquil; for as if hanging between heaven and earth, now to this, now to that opinion they cling; and at last come to this, that they name their errors — however gross — not defects of faith, but only *opinions* — which is little short of Epicureanism.

Know therefore that things said of God are of two kinds: some **of faith**, and some **beyond faith**. *Of faith*: that God is one in essence, three in persons, omnipotent, just, good, and the like. *Beyond faith*: things which do not directly concern an article of faith, but pertain either to the more obscure works of God, or to the most hidden recesses of Scripture — such as, what did God do before he created heaven and earth? What kind of, or where, is paradise? Where is hell? Where now are Enoch and Elijah? Which sort of questions Augustine (*Confessions* xi, c. 30) says are of those men *who thirst for evil rather than for the capacity to know*.

In these matters, one may *opine* — nay, be ignorant, saving the Christian faith. But **in things which are of faith, it is not enough to entertain some opinion** — the soul must be as fully persuaded as may be that what we hold is most true.

The reasons of this assertion are four:

**(i)** First, in matters of faith we are commanded not merely as it is in the Creed, but Scripture says: *He that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him* (Heb 11:6). And Paul writes: *with the heart man believeth unto righteousness* (Rom 10:10). Therefore *faith* is required, not opinion.

**(ii)** Second, faith has for its foundation the sacred Scripture, which does not admit of opinions but requires full assent: *thy Word is truth* (John 17:17). *Blessed are they that heard as unto a lamp that shineth in a dark place* (2 Pet 1:19). Who therefore believes nothing certain in matters of faith but only opines, calls into doubt the Scripture itself — that is, God's truth — which cannot be done with sound piety and unimpaired conscience.

**(iii)** Third, if opining were enough, our worship would never please God — for such opinions can never establish the conscience; and what is done with doubting conscience cannot please God.

**(iv)** Fourth, the heart of man must be certain in his faith, so that he may stand fast in temptations, which are not removed by opinions merely probable about God and divine things.

*Everyone therefore should see what he believes.* *For what simplicity is that of ignorance — not knowing what one believes?* (Jerome, *Contra Luciferianos*.) Every man should lay for the foundation of his faith some Word of Scripture from which he may frame a solid argument for his faith, whereon conscience may rest — and let him not care for reason's cavils, which offer nothing solid but only make the conscience scrupulous, which nothing obliges. Well then wrote Fulgentius (*Ad Donatum*): *Not all who are partakers of Christ, in responding also must express what they believe. But that also is a part of victory when someone cannot defend truth in speech, yet by heart avoids error.* Augustine's saying is well known: *A faithful heart is greatly helped, to know what is to be believed, even if disputing skill is not able to refute the contrary.*

### Case IV. Suppose the certitude of faith rests on Scripture as its solid principle, and faith comes by hearing of the Word of God (Rom 10:17). Are then all things which are heard from the doctors of the Church simply to be believed, without any contradiction whatever?

**Respondeo.** Modern **Enthusiasts** cast a scruple upon consciences here. Nicolaus Weigelius, in his little book *Dialogi Disputatoriorum*, vehemently urges that those who wish to learn celestial truth ought not to contradict their teachers, but as if in themselves dead and unfeeling, believe everything the teachers teach — meaning by "teachers" those of his own order, who boast internal revelations of the Spirit, and so under the name of *spirituals*, are puffed up in the School of the Holy Spirit.

And indeed the *simplicity of faith* which Paul commends (2 Cor 11:3) seems to require that we assent to our doctors without contradiction: for contradictions produce doubts, and make faith uncertain. On which account Christ says of the contradicting Pharisees, *my word hath no place in you* (John 8:37) — i.e., because of your contradictions. And indeed, in the recognition of truth, the Capernaites' were badly off, because they did not simply admit Christ's speech but murmured (John 6:60). Contrariwise, John says: *Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God* (1 John 4:1).

This scruple can be removed by a distinction of contradiction. Some is **licit**, and non-necessary in matters of faith — when for the sake of learning something is opposed to what is very difficult for us, especially where at first sight we have not yet heard some Word of Scripture on which our faith may rest. Here indeed it is lawful to inquire and object, provided the mind be brought docile — which from the Word seeks better instruction than it received, and no longer struggles but acquiesces in the Word.

Reasons for this assertion:

**1.** Nowhere has God commanded us to give immediate assent to our doctors in all things; rather he wills that we *prove all things* (1 Thess 5:21) and try the spirits whether they are of God (1 John 4:1). *Beware of false prophets* (Matt 7:15) — which cannot be done without contradiction.

**2.** The most holy men, whose authority in teaching was plainly divine, permitted themselves to be contradicted — how much more must the doctors of the Church admit contradictions and objections, whose authority is not to be compared with theirs. Christ himself the Pharisees and Sadducees contradicted, whose disputations on various matters he could tolerate (Matt 19:3, 22:23–28, 15:1–2; Mark 11:28); yet nowhere did he rebuke them for these oppositions. The Apostles Peter and John were contradicted in the Council at Jerusalem (Acts 4:7), which the Apostles did not blame but rather rendered account of their faith to the interrogators. The Apostle Paul, after his conversion, was contradicted by the Jews — whom he did indeed admit, but by responding confounded (Acts 9:22). Also Paul disputed in the synagogues (Acts 17:2, 18:19) at Thessalonica, Corinth, and Ephesus.

**3.** Even the angel in a plainly singular matter, which the human understanding could not grasp, admitted contradiction from the Blessed Virgin Mary: *How shall this be?* (Luke 1:34) — which contradiction, as Augustine expounds (Serm. 74), was not of doubting but of admiring, because she was wondering at the counsel of God, that from a virgin a mother should be made, from a human a God born. Such admiration can consist with faith, not removing but illustrating it.

**4.** No one can prohibit contradictions in matters of faith, because *faith is not the work of men but of God* (John 6:29), and *the Gospel is the power of God to salvation to everyone that believeth* (Rom 1:16). Nor is faith always and in all men equally firm, but often has many obstacles and doubts, which yet do not wholly remove it. *For my strength is made perfect in weakness* (2 Cor 12:9). To prohibit contradictions in matters of faith is to force consciences to faith not to persuade it but to impose — which no doctor of the Church ought to arrogate to himself. For not even Paul willed to *cast a snare* upon consciences (1 Cor 7:35), and Peter forbade the pastors to *lord it over the clergy* (1 Pet 5:3). God alone is Lord of consciences. For these causes contradictions of hearers are not to be forbidden — provided that in the manner of question of grace they are moderated, as those which rather augment than diminish faith.

Then there are certain **illicit** contradictions — disputations of reason pertinaciously opposed to the Word, which for that very reason is contradicted because reason cannot grasp the Word, nor will submit itself to the Word: such were those of the Capernaites, saying *This is a hard saying — who can hear it?* (John 6:60), and Nicodemus's too gross retorting to Christ (John 3:4). Here reason forges contradictions in matters of faith, though it has no place — because reason in these matters is blind, and out of its principles opposes what Paul calls the *ἀντιθέσεις τῆς ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως* (1 Tim 6:20) — *the oppositions of falsely-called knowledge* — in which while it pertinaciously persists, it at last degenerates into obduration with blasphemy conjoined, which happened to the Jews contradicting in the synagogue (Acts 13:45) and to those in the School at Jerusalem contradicting Stephen (Acts 7:57), whence at last a manifest sin against the Holy Ghost. This is reason in the sacred a *mere raving*.

These are the hostile contradictions — not of learning, but of assailing and reclamation — which very greatly hurt faith, for they oppose to the divine Word for other obstacles of reason, which Paul calls *ζητήσεις* — *disputes* — which simply oppose faith (Rom 14:10).

Hence there is a *manner* of contradiction: and since about matters of faith from the Word of God alone something certain can be taught and learned, let the pious mind be content — and be rightly instructed by the Word, though reason should always have something to bark. As the ancient distich has it:

> *In matters, wherein certain limits stand,*
> *Beyond which endures nothing right.*

From immoderate oppositions, at last, come contentions, which Paul calls *carnal* (1 Cor 3:3); and elsewhere he writes that the Church is *not contentious* (1 Cor 11:16); *nor let anything be done through strife* (Phil 2:3); *for contention is of those who are proud and know nothing* (1 Tim 6:4).

### Case V. Whether it suffices the believer to hold an *implicit* faith of God and divine things

*Implicit faith is the faith of the Church*, to which Papists ascribe very much, though even in this question they do not agree in all things among themselves.

By the *Church* they understand their prelates — or rather, the sole Pope, into whom every judgment of the Church is resolved. For as Bellarmine writes (*De Romano Pontifice* iv, c. 3): *That infallibility is not in the college of Cardinals, or in a council of Bishops, but in the Pope alone.* He who therefore simply believes what the Pope proposes to the Church to be believed — although he does not know what he believes — has the faith of the Church, or implicit faith, which by others is called *carbonaria* (charcoal-burner's faith), which Hosius Cardinal (*Adversus Prolegomena Brentii* iii) so commends that he calls it a *most safe asylum, in which more faithful help is found than in the exercise of all the Scriptures*.

Hence that blind obedience which their fathers commend to those bidden to believe. Those in the Roman Church, who are ordered to believe whatever they hear — though they do not understand, nor need to understand, but to depend on the labor of superiors, as ones half-witted. From this darkness not even the most keen-sighted and wisest of princes have they excluded. So writes Cassander (*De sensu Motu de ecclesia*): *the prince, in matters of religion, ought to be blind, and see with the eyes of prelates.* So in the Roman Catechism the first question is: *What is a Catholic Christian?* And it is answered: *He who believes whatever the Roman Catholic Church believes, whether written in the Bibles or not.* And even now from those who cling stubbornly to the papacy, though they can defend it with no pretext, it is frequently heard that they *believe what the Church believes*: which is that veil laid over their eyes lest they should acknowledge the truth openly shown. If we fall to the utmost, they impute all fault to the prelates of the Church, from which they suppose themselves to be immune.

**But such faith attracts ruin to many, for the conscience by no means can rest, unless one has known most exactly what he ought to believe of God and divine things.**

**1.** First, the sacred letters require of every man his proper faith: *the just shall live by his faith* (Hab 2:4) — which is as true of justifying faith as of the persuasion of things to be believed. For as no one lives by another's soul, no one is prudent by another's soul, but each is wise by his own soul — so no one can be faithful by another's faith, but each by his own.

**2.** Then Scripture bids us not simply to depend on the labor of doctors, but to *try the spirits whether they are of God* (1 John 4:1); to *beware of false prophets* (Matt 7:15) — which cannot be done without discussion of the proposed doctrine. Hence Basil in his *Ethics* writes (rule 72): *Subjects, who are trained in the Scriptures, ought to prove those things which are said by the doctors, and to receive those things which are consonant with the Scriptures, but to reject the foreign — and vehemently to oppose those who persist in such foreign doctrines.*

**3.** It is altogether dangerous to commit faith — on which the salvation of our souls depends — to the judgments of other men, and never seriously to inquire into it oneself. For unless it be certain that the Church to which you trust does not err, nowhere safely will your conscience rest in temptations. Ever the mind will return: *What if the faith of the Church you profess is false? What if the prelates of the Church be false-doctors, whom Christ bid us beware?* Necessary therefore is discussion and examination of the faith which the Church professes — which cannot be drawn from any other source than from *the Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures*, for upon them the Apostle writes the Church to be founded (Eph 2:20).

**4.** The Berhoeans would not believe what Paul believed, although he was an Apostle indeed — but *searched the Scriptures* whether these things were so (Acts 17:11). How then would anyone without further examination believe the prelates of the Romans, who are not to be compared with the Apostle Paul? *Simplicity of faith* indeed has its praise, but *prudence* Christ also requires (Matt 10:16), *because many false prophets have gone out into the world* (1 John 4:1).

**5.** All are commanded to be *fully persuaded in their own mind* of what they believe (Rom 14:5); all are to *examine themselves whether they be in the faith, and whether Christ Jesus be in them* (2 Cor 13:5); all are to be *ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh a reason of the hope that is in them* (1 Pet 3:15). How can these Apostolic precepts have place in those who see only with foreign eyes, ignorant themselves of what they believe?

**6.** Implicit faith takes away all care of the young. What is the use, then, of laboring at the Catechism, of teaching the ignorant, that each may hold his own faith, if it suffices to believe simply what the Church believes, even in ignorance of what she believes?

*Objection of Gregor. de Valentia* (in his book on Faith c. 15): It is nothing (as Augustine writes) but the authority of the Catholic Church by which one comes to wisdom. And this Catholic authority is greater than the authority of the sectarians — therefore this rather than that ought to receive faith. He illustrates this by the example of a prudent artisan, merchant, or nobleman who, if he prefers the Catholic Church to the sectarians on account of the greater authority of Catholics, God will have nothing to lay to his charge at that dread tribunal against this unlettered man — for as by inquiring into doctrine to come to the knowledge of truth, God did not require of him, since he did not understand theological controversies. So Gregory of Valencia disputes for his implicit faith.

But in fact, *he falsely proposes the external authority of the Church for the inquisition of truth*. For in temptations the conscience is not established by any authority of men, but by God's Word alone; men can lie and deceive, but God is very truth and never fails. So Christ, sending the Jews as it were to a crossroads — whether they should follow the Pharisees or Christ — does *not* refer them to the external authority of the Pharisaic Church (which then was greater than Christ's), but bids them *search the Scriptures* which testify of him (John 5:39).

**As for Augustine** — he speaks of the miraculous nativity, operation, death, and resurrection of Christ; this he calls a most celebrated authority, which moves men to hasten to wisdom. But nothing does he say of the authority of men in the Church, as appears from the context.

Wonderful it is, indeed, that God at his dread tribunal should have nothing to answer to a man setting up merely human authority against his Word, as if from a tripod rashly. Christ did *not* say: *If ye follow greater authority of men.* But: *If ye continue in my Word, then are ye my disciples indeed* (John 8:31). And not by the authority of men but by his Word will he judge in that dread day, as it is written: *The Word which I have spoken, the same shall judge him in the last day* (John 12:48). It remains to our conclusion that the *implicit faith* of the Romans does not suffice for salvation.

### Case VI. Whether therefore the simple layman is bound to know all and each of the articles of faith explicitly

**Respondeo.** In this question the scholastics disagree. Some think it suffices, if the private and rude person implicitly and in general believes whatever the Church believes, though he believe nothing at all explicitly and specifically — as Azor holds (*Institutiones morales* viii, c. 6, q. 1).

Others deem it sufficient if the laity explicitly believe there is one God, rewarder of all the just and of good works, and avenger of the evil, while other articles are believed implicitly — which is the opinion of Hostiensis, Johannes Andreas, and Panormitanus (*De summa Trinitate et fide Catholica*).

Others hold that laymen ought to believe explicitly the articles of faith, at least those which the Church publicly celebrates, proposes, and teaches — such as the article of the most sacred Trinity, the articles concerning the human nature of Christ our Lord (*conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered, was crucified, dead, buried, rose again from the dead, ascended into heaven*) — which is Bonaventure's, Durandus's, and is called the *common* opinion.

Still others contend that any lay person, even the rude and unlearned, ought to know the Apostles' Creed. Others think that such laymen cannot be compelled to learn the Apostles' Creed, and that it suffices if they know the articles of faith as proposed by the Theologians — in this later opinion is Azor (*Instit. morales* viii, c. 6, q. 4).

There are also those who think that if one be of a very hebetic and obtuse ingenuity, it suffices to believe explicitly the clearer articles, and to believe implicitly the rest which he cannot attain — believing what the Church believes; e.g., one who cannot perceive the article of the Trinity, it would suffice him to believe explicitly Christ the Son of God, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered, died, etc.

**We judge that whatever things are necessary to salvation to be obtained or preserved must be known even by the rude, unlearned, and unskilled laity.** For no man can have care of his own salvation who is ignorant of the principles and means of salvation. And these are comprised in the *Catechetical doctrine*, which the Apostle touches (Heb 6:1–2), where he enumerates its chief heads: *repentance from dead works* (which pertains to the Decalogue); *faith toward God*; *the doctrine of baptisms*; *laying on of hands* (i.e., the benediction of the newly-baptized); *resurrection of the dead*; *and eternal judgment*. This doctrine he calls the *elements of the beginning of the oracles of God* — to be proposed to the simpler folk who *have need of milk, not of strong meat* (Heb 5:12); and he calls it *the word of the beginning of Christ, and the foundation* (Heb 6:1). Necessary therefore he judged that the rude be exercised in this doctrine.

But since not every one has the same *ingenious capacity* or occasion of learning, distinction must be made here between the *substance* of the articles of faith, and the *disputations* thereupon which have accrued for the sake of explication. The substance of the articles of faith every layman ought to and can hold; but the disputations and explications are not required of all.

*What is the substance of the articles of faith?* It is that which simply — though generally and confusedly by the words of the article — is signified: e.g., that God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three Gods, but one God in three persons; if one believes this in general, it suffices, though he cannot say specifically what a *person* is, what the personal properties are, and how these differ among themselves — for these things pertain to the schools of the learned, and to the clearer explication of this article. So it suffices for the rude and unskilled man to know that in Christ are two natures, human and divine; that the Son of the Most High is called the Son of Mary; that the Lord of glory was crucified — all which Scripture says of Christ in concept-words, though he does not exactly understand the mystery of the personal union and of the communication of idioms, nor grasps what is disputed of them — for these too pertain to the schools of the learned. And so of the rest.

Then, many things are implicitly believed by the rude which are not expressed in explicit words of faith — which suffices, provided they do not expressly contradict. So he who believes God to be omnipotent and his Father, believes also that he cares for human affairs, and that not only by power and might but also *by his essence* is present to us. He who acknowledges the perfection of the Decalogue, implicitly confesses also the corruption of his nature; for the Decalogue also forbids interior concupiscence of the heart. He who hears in baptism that we are regenerated does not deny that we are born in sins — for regeneration is of those born in sins.

Since these things are so, necessity demands that every householder in his house, and every parish priest in his parish, diligently inculcate the catechetical doctrine to the ruder ones — which those who ignore are in great danger; and they will suffer penalties of their negligence who neglect those committed to their care in this respect.

Great was the diligence used in this heretofore, when the ruder ones, especially catechumens, on the day they were to be baptized were held to publicly recite the Creed and the Lord's Prayer — as Augustine testifies (*Sermon 42 ex quinquaginta*). And in the *Consecratio* (dist. 4, c. 41) it says: *Before all things, are recited words from another sermon of St. Augustine*, in which he exhorts sponsors that *before all things they hold the Creed and the Lord's Prayer, and inculcate the same to those whom they took up from the sacred font.* In the Council of Foroiuliense under Charles Pius, it was decreed: *Every Christian ought to hold the Creed and the Lord's Prayer as a memorized rule of faith* — *both sexes and every condition, male, female, young, old, servants, freemen, boys, unmarried, married, wife, and virgin, who by this hereditary rule cannot come into any part of the celestial kingdom.* Hence in our times, even in the villages, public catechetical examinations are held. And Luther everywhere, especially in the preface to the Small Catechism, urges this exercise — so that he holds those who refuse to learn the catechetical doctrine as apostates who deny Christ, and are therefore not to be admitted to the Sacred Supper, nor to sponsorship at baptism, nor to any part of the office of Christ.

### Case VII. What if someone through defect of faithful instruction and of the articles is entirely ignorant — is his hope of salvation not utterly despaired?

**Respondeo.** It may happen that some are wholly without care or knowledge of divine things, either because they were ill-educated, orphaned early of their parents, or utterly neglected by them, or because they grew up in fields, forests, or among cattle, or even from earliest childhood dwelt among barbarians and men estranged from the Christian faith. Their ignorance some think to be without sin and *invincible*, as they call it — in which opinion is Jesuit Azor (*Instit. moral.* viii, c. 3, q. 3).

**But if we wish to follow the sound rule of the divine Word, we cannot subscribe to that opinion.** For Christ our Saviour places eternal life in the knowledge of himself and of the heavenly Father (John 17:3); God the Father also places our righteousness in the knowledge of his Son (Isa 53:11). *Whoever, then, is without Christ, ignores also the Father* — according to that word: *He that honoureth not the Son, honoureth not the Father which hath sent him* (John 5:23; cf. John 5:15). How then can they have hope of eternal life?
