### Case VI. Whether the human nature in Christ is rightly honored by us with divine worship, so that our faith and our prayers may be directed also to it

**Respondeo.** If I consider the *human nature in Christ separately* in its own properties, by no means is it of the same state, glory, condition, and power as the nature of the *Word* — for this indeed would be a synergism of the divinity. For by this reasoning the creature would be equated with the Creator, and by union with the flesh some accession made to the most simple essence of the divinity. Therefore considered thus separately, no worship is owed to it — nay, considered separately outside the *Logos*, it does not subsist anywhere, since it has no proper subsistence.

So *Cyril* considered Christ's human nature when in *De recta fide ad Theodosium* he wrote: *the divinity in Christ is being adored; the humanity adoring, as also the Lord himself says (John 4): we adore what we know.* And Augustine's memorable sentence (*On Psalm* 98) *of the great Lord Jesus. In Christ the humanity is prayed to, because the divinity is received and united to the divinity. If you separate a man from God, as the Photinians or the Samosatenes, — either I never believe, or I serve, as if I found a garment, or a purple, or a royal diadem lying: shall I dare to adore, when the King has been clothed with it, and to incur danger of death, if I contemn to adore it at once with the King?*

**False therefore is what Thomas writes (III q. 25 art. 1): *the same person of Christ is to be adored by the adoration of Latria for his divinity, and by the adoration of Dulia for the perfection of his humanity.***

*One is the adoration of Christ*, which Scripture knows — which is proper to the Word by essence, and befits the flesh united to him by grace. Nor does the human nature of Christ outside the *Logos* subsist anywhere; therefore neither can it be worshipped in any way outside him. When therefore I consider it *united to the Logos*, and constituting one person with him, then I consider it as *partaker of the divine majesty, omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence, nay, of the very hypostasis of the Word*.

Therefore in this consideration, from the cult and veneration owed to the *Logos*, it can in no way be exempted; but what worship is given to the *Logos through his nature*, here to the human nature is *attributed through the grace of union*. Whence also it itself is the *object of faith, confidence, adoration, and every divine worship*, which is owed to the *Logos*.

It is not however to be worshipped separately *as with the Logos*, as if it stands by itself, as *Nestorius* wanted, who therefore is called *ἀνθρωπολάτρης* in the Code of Justinian (i, tit. 1, ss. 5). But in the *Logos* it is worshipped with *one worship*, and adored with *one adoration*, as Cyril (Ep. 10 against Nestorius) explains: *not another, in whom is present, is worshipped simultaneously with another; but one Christ Jesus is worshipped with one proper adoration by him*. And Damascene (*De fide orth.* iii, c. 8) writes: *I adore the Logos with his flesh — that is, the whole Christ — because of the flesh being united to the Deity conjoined*.

**Reasons of this our faith:**

**1.** Because the human nature of Christ with the *Logos* constitutes one person, from which it is never dissolved, outside which it is nowhere found. Divine worship is not of one nature only, but of the *whole person*, in the manner in which we believe such a Son of God to have been born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, etc. Hence Leo (*Ep.* 10) writes: *nor without true divinity is humanity, nor without true humanity is divinity believed.* And Cyril: *De recta fide ad Theodosium: not the bare Word alone we believe, despoiling him of flesh, nor as a *mere man* like us; but faith terminates in a natural and true God in the person of Christ*.

**2.** Because in the worship of Christ we look not only to the *person*, but also to his *office*, which is common to each nature. When about God the question is, it is rightly said: God alone is to be worshipped and adored; but when about the worship of Christ it is asked, not only the person, as *infinite and eternal principle* is considered, but also and especially as *redeemer, propitiator, Saviour, King, and our mediator* — those offices are of each nature: as *the man Christ our mediator is called* (1 Tim 2:5), and *God in Christ reconciled himself to us* (2 Cor 5:19).

**3.** Scripture teaches us to be baptized not only into the divine nature of Christ, but also into his death (Rom 6:3). As therefore we are baptized, so we believe: which is the collation of *Basil, Nazianzen*, and *Cyril*.

**4.** The human nature of Christ, through union with the *Logos*, deserves to enter the consortium of the Holy Trinity, as Ambrose speaks of the resurrection. Whatever pertains to the Holy Trinity is worthy of divine cult and veneration.

**5.** The human nature of Christ has been *made one* with the *Logos* through exaltation to the right hand of the Father — as Paul speaks (Phil 2:9–10): *he received a name, which is above every name; that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth*.

**6.** Finally, examples are added of those who worshipped Christ as *the son of David* (Luke 18:39; Matt 15, 20); and in the Apocalypse *the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, who was slain, and adored him with the same reverence with which they worshipped him who sat upon the throne* (Rev 5:8, 14).

These all can confirm the conscience that we do not err if in our prayers we approach Christ himself, and direct them to his human nature.

**Nor should certain trivial objections trouble anyone**, from Calvinists — that *cursed is the man who trusts in a man* (Jer 17:5); that *God does not give his glory to another* (Isa 42:8); that *idolaters* are called *those adoring gods who are not by nature gods* (Gal 4:8) — see the *Examen* of Danaeus, pp. 415, 416, 417, 418, 419; and Sturmius in *Prodromus* p. 26.

These are all to be understood of *man* and other creatures *outside* the hypostasis of the *Logos*. For in a bare man surely no confidence is to be placed. But of the man who is himself the *Lord from heaven*, who was born in the Father's own throne, and *exalted to the right hand of the Father's omnipotence and divine virtue*, Scripture pronounces that *whoever confides in him shall not be confounded*.

*(A distinction is to be made between the *true* man and the *mere* man. Christ is *true* indeed, but not *mere* man. Isa 42:8, Jer 17:5, Gal 4:8 speak of *mere idols*, not of a person like *Servus Kupios*, not of a *human* Deus.)*

And since this is so, *the glory of God is not given to another, when in the person of Christ there is not one and another, but is settled with God in solidum the praise and majesty, that he alone is worshipped and adored — not however as of old, of *bare divinity*, but *with his flesh worshipped and glorified* — one in *divine latria*, just as God alone is life-giving and continues, though the flesh of God is life-giving, because it is not of one else who is united, but proper to God alone*.

### Case VII. Can one, without sin, place confidence at the same time in God and in a creature — as often is popularly said: *I trust in God and in my armor; I trust in God and in my ploughing*, etc.

**Respondeo.** Certain it is that, properly speaking, our confidence has no other object than God, who — just as he had commanded that we should have no other gods before him — so also wills us to trust simply in him alone. Therefore in Scripture God is opposed, in whom must trust *every congregation of the people* (Ps 62:9), and *sons of Adam are vain and mendacious* (Ps 62:10). *It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man* (Ps 118:8).

Yet often such expressions are heard, in which what is owed to God alone seems to lean on the creature — as when the soldier says: *I trust God and my armor*; the farmer: *I trust God and my strong arm*; the paterfamilias: *I trust God and my grain*.

Yet it must be known that these are *popular sayings*, in which *καθ᾽ ἀκρίβειαν* is not to be sought, nor is any other object of faith intended between God and creatures — but only that confidence in God is *not immediate, but through an art, through hand, through grain* and similar organs which God gives to each as necessary. For an honest art always feeds the industrious cultivator, who loves and exercises it — and who in the time of necessity uses it for preparing food, does not so much place confidence in the art itself as in *God* acting through this medium.

So God is *the one who teaches the hands of soldiers for battle, and makes bows of brass to break in their arms* (Ps 18:34); who *not without the hand of the soldier, or without arms, gives victory*. He therefore who trusts in his hand, in his sanity, in the strength of his body, does nothing else than trust God, who will strengthen his hands in honest battle, so that he may not fall into the hand of the enemy. And when God through grain feeds men, the paterfamilias trusts God through this medium to provide sustenance for himself and his household.

For God does not want such confidence, which makes men *secure* — as if now, because they have means, God should aid them, wholly without labor: but confidence conjoined with our labor. Therefore *David* orders us to *commend our ways to the Lord and hope in him*, and yet also to *inhabit the earth, and be fed by his wealth* (Ps 37:3–5).

That confidence, therefore, which one has in art, in strength of hand, in his grain, is not properly speaking *faith*, that virtue of the first precept — but only a *comfort and sign of a mind present and tranquil*, which by the presence of those means is more confirmed in its confidence in God.

Otherwise, faith properly so called has as its object only *omnipotent God*, to whom in this cult no one is to be joined; when however anything else is joined to him, it has the ratio of *medium and instrument* through which he operates, not of *organ* — but *only in God*, who operates through it. And this faith properly so called always firmly adheres to God, even if those means are lacking, since it knows God to be not bound to them.

Hence *maledicted are those who trust in man* (Jer 17:5), and much more those who trust in another creature — maledicted are they, since our whole help is from the Lord, who through few can help just as through many, who even without means holds the *fastness of omnipotence*.

We can therefore use those popular sayings in the sense just indicated, especially since we have a similar locution in Scripture. For Prov 31:11, of a virtuous wife it is read: *the heart of her husband trusts in her*; and Exod 14:31, of the people is said *that they feared the Lord and believed in the Lord and in Moses his servant*. The object of faith is God alone, yet they are said to have *believed in God and in Moses* — because so long as they had faith in the words of Moses, their confidence in the Lord was confirmed.

### Case VIII. The chief part of internal worship is love: it is asked, when man loves God so that his conscience may rest, that he has satisfied the divine command

**Respondeo.** Before all things it is here to be held that *love toward God, from every point perfect and absolute, to which nothing can be added, in no mortal in this age is found.* For the command about loving God is so lofty that human nature vitiated by the flesh is far less and weaker than that to be able to satisfy it. For Moses says: *thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy strength* (Deut 6:5) — which Christ called the *first and greatest* commandment (Matt 22:38).

The Papists acknowledge that *to love God with all one's heart is truly the same as to keep God's commands, or certainly the one is necessarily connected with the other, since it cannot happen that he who loves God with all his heart, does not also keep all his commandments* — that indeed Bekan confesses in his *Disp. de just. bonorum operum* c. 15.

Since however *perfect obedience to divine commands* in man in this life is impossible, we teach, and hence they seek certain emblems, that even of that precept about loving God with all the heart, they show its possibility — with all which nevertheless the conscience about the true love of God cannot be satisfied.

*Stapleton* (lib. 6 *de just.* c. 24) and Gregory of Valencia (lib. 3 *de virtutibus* q. 3) write: *the precept of loving God with all the heart is doctrinal, not obligatory* — with which nearly coincides what Bellarmine writes (*De monachis* i, c. 13): *this precept is given as it were as a scope, not that it be fulfilled: but if even it be not fulfilled, one is not made a transgressor.*

But truly these are too crude, to which a pious man could easily oppose: *he cannot understand how any command should not oblige but only teach; for every precept is a particle of the law, and the law from *obligating* has its name; and it is absurd that any law be given, which does not oblige those to whom it is given.*

**Yet no less difficult to understand is how any precept may be given by God, which ought not be fulfilled** — every precept rather is given that it be fulfilled; therefore every transgression of the law is called *sin* (1 John 3:4) because it is not conformable to the precept. And God expressly says of the precepts: *hear, ye people, do these precepts of God; if you do them not, malediction shall be intimated to you* (Deut 27:26).

**Bellarmine** writes: *to love God with all one's forces and with all one's heart does not signify all forces at once but with one's whole heart, but only *for one's forces of loving* — sed *with special love*.* But this liberation is easily persuaded to the pious mind, because it plainly fights with the words of the Lord, who does not say *for the ability of your forces*, but *ex totis viribus* — thou shalt love God, *ex toto corde*, requiring all the powers of the soul by which God is loved, so that all our knowing, willing, and being able is referred to God. For to himself God has destined the whole man, as it were to his glory. *Nothing to a total remains, which can be added to a total; because if anything remained, it would not be a total* — says Augustine (*De spiritu et litera* c. 36).

The same *Bellarmine* writes: this precept about loving God is doctrinal, *which does not oblige at every time but only when its glory needs to be procured*. So says Toletus (iv, c. *confess.* c. 9). But even in this emblem the pious mind cannot rest, since no time can be given in which the glory of God is not to be promoted by us. Even if therefore in its exercise external love is not carried into God at every moment, yet in its *habit and end* it always looks to him — as *whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do all to the glory of God* (1 Cor 10:31). When therefore we love parents, children, and friends, and do them good, then we love God for whose sake all things are to be loved which can be dear to us. Whence Augustine says (*Confessions*): *the more I love thee, O God, the more anything else I love, which for thy sake I love*.

**Becan** writes in *Disp. de just. hon. operum* c. 31: *to love God above all things is when we prefer him to other things, and neither from love or fear of any creature offend God, nor are drawn back by love of him.* Which indeed is true, but not sufficient — for the love of God requires *rectitude of all forces, and plentifulness of the offices owed to God*, such as does not fall into corrupt nature.

**These things therefore cannot satisfy consciences. For they flow from a *vitiated principle* — as if in this life we could perfectly fulfill the law, which Scripture in many places denies (of which elsewhere): who indeed will give a man such a mind, that he may fear God, and keep all his commandments at every time?** (Deut 5:29).

**Far better is conscience counseled if we acknowledge our imperfection**, love God as much as is in us, submit all our things to him, cling to him alone, and if no retribution appear, but afflictions daily grow, we do not depart from love. So in all these, even when we contend toward the highest, let us deplore our defects, certain believing that God will not impute them to us for Christ's sake, and in whatever effort of ours proceeding from faith in Christ, he will paternally rest. For as Bernard (*Sermon 50 on the Canticles*) says: *by commanding impossibles God has not made prevaricators of men, but humble — that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world become guilty before God.*

— ❦ —

## Chapter VI. On Cases of Conscience Concerning the External Cult of God in General

*De casibus conscientiae circa cultum Dei externum in genere.*

God requires this cult from us equally with the internal, since he must be loved with all our forces — therefore all our conversations, gestures, and works ought to testify of our confidence in God and our love. And as Christ is the redeemer of both our soul and body, so also to each is required a direction toward God. Wherefore Paul exhorts (1 Cor 6:20): *glorify God in your body, and in your spirit.*

The external cult of God is called by Greek *religio*, from *religando*, and by common usage of the vulgar *religion* — of which either it is exercised *publicly* by all, or *privately* in each family. **Public** exercise of religion consists in the preservation of pure religion in some commonwealth; in the maintenance of public congregation; in the hearing of the Word; in public prayers; in the use of the sacraments. **Private** in domestic discipline; in the exercises of piety among children and servants; in the preservation of an innocent life; and the most sweet conjunction of the domestics, that God with one voice they may worship.

Just as internal cult concerns the first precept of the Decalogue, so external cult concerns the second and third — and embraces invocation, vows, oaths, the treatment of the Word and sacraments, and things like these. Of these particular parts of external religion we shall see later; and now of those cases which occur about the external cult of God in general we shall treat.

### Case I. Whether care of true religion in the state is necessary — so that it cannot be omitted with safe conscience

**Respondeo.** In paganism there were not a few who were learned indeed but *atheists* — Lucretius, Diagoras, Lucianus, and their followers — who imagined that public and private affairs are agitated by chance and fortune without any government or providence of divinity, and that no god is to be worshiped.

Others said *the cult of divinity was invented by political counsel* — that men, at least by fear of the gods, might be concordant in the community of justice, and enjoy peace and security in private things (which one dared not otherwise despoil from another), and might avail themselves felicitously in public — as Plutarch mentions in his book *De placitis Philosophorum*.

But *the wiser Philosophers judged that the commonwealth cannot be governed without a numen, nor be happy without religion of the numen*. Therefore *Aristotle* (*Politics* vii, c. 8) among the things without which a state cannot exist, first places the preservation of the divine cult. *Plato* also (*Republic* i) says that *the chief care in the commonwealth is to be undertaken concerning religion*.

For religion is the *true foundation of the state, the origin of justice and probity*. For *he lives ill who does not believe God well*, as Augustine (*De civ. Dei* v, c. 10). And Cicero (*De natura deorum* i): *when reverence of God is shaken out of the minds of men, all things are filled with inhumanity and wickedness.*

Religion is the *bond of laws and honest discipline*, as Plato names it (*Republic* iv, and *De legibus* vi). *God has infused into the minds of men the discrimination of the honest and the base*, and by reverence of the numen holds many in office who would otherwise, with all shame cast away, easily perpetrate turpitude.

Religion is the *cause of divine benediction*: as we cultivate God, so also he blesses the commonwealth: *the Lord will be with you, when you are with him. If you seek him, he will be found by you: but if you forsake him, he will forsake you also* (2 Chr 15:2). *God will care for us, if we suffer ourselves to be cared for by him. No one does God desert, unless first deserted by him.*

Religion is finally the *impediment of confusion in the commonwealth*. For when no one cares what religion each professes, either they become atheists — who say in their heart, *there is no God* — or Epicureans, who hold all religions in promiscuous, or they become impious with idolatrous superstitions, which introduce right on confusions and rush to the overturning of the commonwealth. Whence Plato (*De legibus* x) said: *ignorance of the true God is the most present plague of the commonwealth*.

Therefore, if we would have a *quiet and pacified commonwealth*, if we hope for happy successes of our affairs, if we would provide well for us and our posterity — the first care ought to be of *religion*, since *when this is well-cared-for, all conditions of the commonwealth are advanced*. This is the sum of all the Fathers in their epistles to Timothy and Titus (Cyprian, etc.).

Hither pertain the *prayers proposed to the people at the sacrifices* concerning kings (1 Tim 2:2) and the exhortation to penitence (from the example of the priests, Joel 2:17). By this reasoning, on the part of the ministers of the Church, the purity of religion can be preserved.

Nor should it disturb thee, that what has been said needs to be nourished and confirmed, so that it be not agitated by any wind of court fans. This true religion is to be preserved for us and our posterity.

### Case II. Whether more than one religion in the commonwealth can be tolerated with safe conscience

**Respondeo.** This question is variously disputed by Theologians and politicians. Where the extremes on each side are sometimes overshoot — for there are some who simply and without any consideration of circumstances do not admit multiple religions in a commonwealth, because God once willed that in Israel one religion at least be observed; because the Israelite laws destroyed the groves and shrines of the gentiles in order to retain in the people one religion; because from a multitude of religions the origin of dissension is the diversity of religion; because *liberty of believing is liberty of erring*, and things similar — of which see Bellarmine (*De laicis* iii, c. 19).

Others think this doctrine altogether too strict, and therefore not only do not prohibit multiple religions in the commonwealth, but even admit them willingly. So *Diodorus Siculus* records of the Egyptians (i, c. 8): they introduced *diverse and mixed religion* for the sake of stabilizing the empire, and lest all the Egyptians should ever conspire together. And in *Bellum Gallicum* vi, Apud Diodorum, it is added, no monarchy was destroyed but by that same reason which imposes no matter of religion; but the contrary is shown in the West, where the summit-cutting party over religion is now seen to be gaping. And in *Turcicus Sultan* Seiimus it is referred: that to root out Christians and others alien from the Turkish religion, in a low-lying way he sent an ambassador various flowers together born and ornamenting the garden, from a common little window, and inquired: through which manner is such variety of herbs and flowers not only not harmful, but wonderfully recreates the eyes and senses? — thus in my empire diverse faith and religion is nothing else than nature and manner of speech, in which each may live safely. Vives (*Comment. in Aug. de civ. Dei* i, c. 32).

However, to counsel conscience in this part, most safely to hold the *middle way*. For if to us it were always permitted to live according to our vow and desire, nothing indeed were more to be wished than *unity of religion*, that with one number we should worship God, and among us so many *fingers* dispersed by innovation should be as one hand. Nothing so distracts the souls of men as diversity of religion — since, on the contrary, the best foundation of concord is agreement in religion. Wherefore the magistrate as much as possible should give effort, that the purity of true religion be preserved in his dominions, and every innovation be avoided — as Philo the Philosopher rightly said, that it is decreed everywhere among nations not to change or violate the ancestral religion.

Therefore among all it is agreed, that the magistrate *sins gravely* against GOD if he induces various religions (which he could have prevented) into the commonwealth voluntarily, admits them, favors them, or without any necessity retains them. For he does nothing else than resist the counsel of God — that *unity of religion* should be *preserved* — and introduces the *destruction of all the pillars of the commonwealth* which are of religion.

*Wherefore Theodosius the second* judged that a magistrate who admits adventitious religions is a subverter of the commonwealth and a secret betrayer of his country, and to be deprived of the right and dignity of governing not only his own dominion, but even his kingdom and dominions which come into the possession of those who, at his suggestion, freely and without a call are able to profess Christ.

Where however the religion of the state is *diverse*, not indeed admitted spontaneously, but nonetheless already in the commonwealth of many adherents is occupied *without motion of sedition*, false religions cannot be extirpated: then they must be *tolerated*, meanwhile with more diligent purer-doctrine doctors, and if the rest be conveyed to nothing, others adhering nonetheless to purer religion may be preserved *like lilies among thorns*. For it is better to have some pure religion, than none at all, and less inconvenient in the commonwealth to have many religions than one which is impure or utterly wrong.

**When the empire of the magistrate is not sole but *mixed***, that is, when the estates of the realm partake with him in imperial power — the higher magistrate cannot introduce false religions into his rule alone, nor abolish the true. So he must leave the *free exercise* of religion to his subjects, and *inferior magistrates* also should not be diverted from a good work. Therefore against a higher magistrate — not only as fellow-workers, but even to license him — subjects must confess, when the work is necessary, that they are Centurions and Princes of the people despoiling and tyrannically ruling (Acts 23:11); or previously by prayers, by intercessions, by other means, if need be, they should defend it, that he not decree things pleasing to the magistrate contrary to God and his will.

**When by fundamental laws of Empire the magistrate has bound himself to observation of a diverse religion, then in the tolerance of the diverse religions of his own faith, in his obligation is comprehended without peril of perjury and with safe conscience, he can attempt nothing.** So the Emperor is bound to leave the religion of the Evangelicals free in the Roman Empire, because of the *Pacification of Passau* (year 1552), and in the councils and treaties of the Empire, both by the vote of the Papists and of the Evangelicals and by the assent of the Emperor, he confirmed and settled fundamental laws (which are called *Capitulationes*), by which in the election of a new Emperor these are confirmed and to the same imperial obligation stand.

**In these cases it is not lawful for the magistrate to abolish diverse religions from the commonwealth, but to tolerate them; and if he tolerates them, three cautions ought to be exercised:**

**1.** *That open blasphemies against God, against Christ, against the most blessed his mother be not tolerated* — such as are found in the Turkish and Jewish religions; such blasphemies are to be severely coerced.

**2.** *That from toleration of diverse religions no syncretism arise.* Wherefore for the sake of political peace men are commanded at least *not to unite* with those of the same profession. As Samaritans were once prohibited (2 Kgs 17:24), so *syncretism* in religion is prohibited, not indeed sometimes in political concord; but the *mixing of faith itself* is not to be admitted at any time, since it has the appearance of denial. It hurts especially this verse:

> *One is the Faith, the Christian religion, one baptism, one bread, one wine, one is the shepherd, one is the Church the mother.*

> *One faith, and one is Christ, one Spirit, one hearts.*

**3.** *For the sake of one salvation more than one commonwealth in these fires* — in prayers, in the hearing of the Word, in the use of sacraments — not even in political affairs is admissible: *of faith, however, at no time is it to be admitted*, because it has the appearance of denial. Bear this verse:

> *Whoever does not conjoin dogmas in Christ, foolish man, is not my brother.*

Nor does the practice of the Church admit this, that ministers of the Church, especially in the negotiation of religion, when they have to deal with adversaries, would join hands to what these do — as at Ratisbon it was once permitted, but where all things ordered by us must not conclude anything against Christ, but rather nothing but a solid foundation.

### Case III. Whether it is lawful to tolerate the *erring* in the commonwealth

**Respondeo.** Here a distinction is to be made among the *erring*: some are *privately erring*, who not only themselves dangerously err in matters of faith, but also disturb others and lead them into their party, propagate their errors, and seduce the simpler ones. These, though not doctors of the Church, are nonetheless not far from *heretics* — of whom it is written that they *stir up wars and dissensions among Christians* (Rom 16:17); that others they *lead astray* (2 Tim 2:17); that they *bring exitial dogmas* (2 Pet 2:1); that not only do they themselves *fall from truth*, but *pervert others* (2 Tim 2:18).

**Such** in the pacified commonwealth are *not to be tolerated* — not indeed be given up *to fire*, as Augustine judges (*De ipsis* — with reference to *Circumcellions*) — where he says: *even until my death of every heresy chastisement should never be inflicted, though the heretic may err* (*Ad Bonifacium* c. 50), but if they do not desist from their institute, they may be *thrown into prison* — that they may there cease from wrangling and thus deprive others of the way of salvation. But if they *conspire* to some sedition and become propagators of their errors and defenders of them, they can even be treated *more harshly*, and the magistrate can proceed even to inflict death upon them. So then Centurions and princes of the people expelled the tyranny of Adramelech (Acts 23:11).

In the time of Augustine, action was taken against the Donatists and *Circumcelliones*, who not only made a peril of doctrine, disseminated their errors, but even took up arms and pursued the orthodox with exquisite punishments (*Ad Bonifacium* c. 50).

*Others are private erring, but of humble mind, who create no scandal, disturb no one, spread no error* — nay rather ready to *give way*, if they can be *better taught*, and moreover *obey the magistrate*, and *do not disturb concord*, since they cling to their opinions *not for sedition or interdicts*. Such are to be borne with, along with others who — as the wise and Latin authors say, and as Chrysostom exhorts in *De sacerdote* c. 4 — should be softly and gently caressed and cured. *Sweeter medicine is that which persuades the will, than that which moves it — as we ought to teach patiently, that they may become better.*

### Case IV. On the toleration of Jews in a Christian commonwealth

**Respondeo.** In the matter of tolerating the Jews, the Theologians are extremely divided. But the following authors patronize *those who deny that they should be tolerated*: Chemnitz *Vita Christi* c. 9, teaches that Jews are not to be tolerated among Christians, so long as they persist in their obstinacy — since he defends himself with these arguments: (1) the reverence which is to be had toward the *blood*, from which Christ is born according to nature; (2) the promise that Christ made to *save Israel*, though *Israel* is not still *the fatherhood of God*; (3) the reasons of the promised conversion at the *end of time*, whence some hope from the promise nor to injure them by any punishment.

Christ himself commands us to *love our enemies* (Matt 5:44); and finally, since if they blaspheme Christ elsewhere less openly, they hurt no more the Christians.

*Those who wish to tolerate them* have this in mind: (1) the *magistrate* is to preserve them among his subjects because he suffered them earlier under certain imperial pledges, and gave himself to us from his heart.

In this regard, the operation of the *ministers of the Church* should be all the more diligently occupied, since Jews as much as possible are to be *reduced to the number of the pious* — as need is, but let us not for greed of gain oppress and squeeze the Jews out of the substance of Christians (from which the Magistrate often, as if from a *sponge*, expresses the Jews) — not without the greatest scandal.

**Nor is the *hope of Jews' conversion* of small moment.** For though we do not envy their conversion, how difficult it is — experience has shown, since Christ inflicted *fourfold malediction* on the Jews (Ps 49:6). One is from God's own justice, which their own mouth pronounced against them at the time of the passion of Christ (Matt 27:25) — *let his blood be upon us and upon our children*. Moreover, since they cannot deny, they were the *people of God* now degenerating; the *true circumcision* — the note of God's people — they still hold to be one (as Luther narrates, Ps 132, Tom. 3, German Iena, fol. 219).

Even though the Jews' conversion is difficult, it is not doubtful that from among them some are converted, and that more are yet to be converted. For Paul more than others teaches (Rom 11:25) about the conversion of the Jews, this mystery to us being new and rich, as it were unheard.

The *inconveniences which follow from their retention* ought not, however, to be so feared that they compare with those which we suffer at *Christians* in whose bosoms they are fostered. For beyond the horrid blasphemies which the *Jews* burn in special manner against Christ and his mother, they contrive against Christians unbearable frauds and usurious pillages, which drive them into destitution.

The *Jewish community*, given permission by Luther, in his *Epistle to Medicine* (Ep. 32), noted that Jews take from Christians as much of their bodily faculties and mind as they can — as also from the *judgment of the Theologians of Giessen* (published year 1615), where the judgment of other theologians is annexed, together with a small tract, further appears: John Lauterbach *Judas Iscariot* pp. 20 *annos*. *A hundred flowers, usury may be 2 nummi Francofurtenses.* They suck the *blood of Christians* — and when they cannot use adults, they *scarcely enter their infamous slaughter halls*, under the species of medicine, which they *never learned*, and *many of the lives of men lay in ambush*. They *poison wells* — and even before the magistrate they daily in prayers seem to place, that they call *Amidah* — *imprecate that God destroy them*. *Antonius Margaritha, a baptized Jew*, affirms of the sanctified Jews that with what they receive from them, they *drown a human name*, thinking that by singular Divine providence they are done, and *let an infallible sign of redemption be*, that from those, whom in their heart they curse with vicissim, they be affected with benefits.

**Which indeed moved *Luther* to judge it most healthful, if from Jews' insults and many other inconveniences we would be immune** — so that in *no cohabitation* to permit ours external, but relegate them to their country, so that they no longer have of what they may complain, that they be *our captives*, or we, that we consult their frauds and usury.

For which cause **long since Christian bishops and magistrates cast them out from the society of Christians**. *Cyril* cast them out about the year of Christ 418 (*Historia Tripartita* xi, c. 33). It is read of Sisebutus, a *Wisigothic king*, who cast out the Jews from Spain about the year of Christ 651 (*Freder* in Chronicles) — and when they there again nested, cast them out again, *Wamba* the king, in number 30,000, about the year of Christ 691, as *Isidore* reports. Cast them out from Gaul, *Dagobert* about the year of Christ 559, referring *Genebrardus*.

Afterward many commonwealths cast them out of their cities: *Nürnberg* — Augsburg — *Elettwang* — Ulm — *Prag*; and it is not unknown of what city; in which oppidum they had erected, and no more do they have but a *place* which from the Jews has a name, and the *image Schemhamphoras* to the ignominy of the Jews *along with the outward parts of the parish temple* has been chiseled in stone, to be exposed to the eyes of all.

*It shall be a happy commonwealth in such matters, when both from Nimrod (tyranny), and from perverse gods, and false witnesses, and worst of all, from Jews* (which since it now grows) shall we be immune. Which if these things could all be done, *diligently observed, the religion of the Jews would fall of itself* to the Christians. But since many magistrates for the sake of *turpitude of gain* indulge Jews' sacred rites too much, such things are to be borne by subjects, who so long as Jews live peacefully among them do not incite them by molestation, nor curse them (who by their own doing are cursed), much less kill them, since concerning them it is written (Ps 59:11): *slay them not, lest my people forget.*

**God preserves the Jews among Christians as our *scribes* and *guardians of the biblical codex*** — as Augustine names them (*Contra Faustum Manich.* xii, c. 24, and *Epistle* 58) — and *are also an example of divine wrath against the contempt of Christ and his Gospel.* Which considering, Bernard writes (*Ep.* 322): *the Jews are not to be persecuted nor slaughtered, but they are necessary to be spared, since certain marks are represented in the Dominical Passion.*

But the magistrate who is such as merely attends to his own private convenience — will render account of this in his time before God, whose sincere cult and *the Jews themselves in their conversion* he impedes, but in impiety and blasphemies he confirms them. *Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil; putting light for darkness, and darkness for light* (Isa 5:20) — this by the faithful ministers of the Church is frequently to be inculcated.

### Case V. Whether one can with good conscience attend the sacred rites of Jews or heretics for the sake of seeing

**Respondeo.** Most grave is the admonition of Paul (1 Cor 6:14): *be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers, for what fellowship hath righteousness with iniquity?* And (Eph 5:11): *have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness*. Also (1 Cor 10:14): *flee from idolatry* — which withdraws all pious ones from consort with the impious, and disjoins confessors of diverse religions in the exercise of religion.

For which cause the office of a pious and constant confessor is to *preserve the deposit of sound doctrine*, of which he is convinced in conscience, so as by no means to pollute, diminish, or altogether abandon it — which happens with those who deal with adversaries of true religion.

Therefore as much as is in us, we ought to *abstain from their sacred rites*, lest either we cause ourselves scruples, or with offense of the weak we seem to *collude* with adversaries. Against this apostolic admonition they doubly sin:

- **First, some of their own motion, no one commanding, thrust themselves into those profane sacred rites, whether because they are Epicureans, who care about no religion, and to whom it is indifferent which sect they join; or because they seek some little gain, which they see they cannot procure unless in religion with others they collude.** These indeed most gravely sin, since only one faith exists, of which everyone in his heart ought to be certain: *whatever is not of faith is sin* (Rom 14:23). And by all means in matters of religion base gain is to be shunned. Such *halt* on both sides; even if they are not Epicureans outright, at minimum yet in religion they are *lukewarm*, whom the grave judgment of the Lord awaits.

- **Second, there are those who put forward the mandate of the magistrate, by which they are compelled to those sacred rites — but since the magistrate is not Lord of conscience or religion, rightly here obedience is denied him.** It must be sought to please God (Acts 5:29). Otherwise a *devotional simulation* here has no place, but rather offends God and men: *no man can serve two masters — either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other* (Matt 6:24). So Paul at Athens entered the idolatrous temple, but did not approve idolatry, but sought only the *occasion* for offering the doctrine of the true God to the idolaters (Acts 17:22 ff.).

**However, in two cases can one, without wounding conscience, attend the sacred rites of infidels or heretics: (1) *to look at* — when one wants only to be a spectator, that of the profanity of infidels or heretics he may testify more surely and truly, as pilgrims enter Jews' synagogues, attend Papist mass, look at their processions, that they may say they saw with their own eyes, what those relating to them scarcely would have believed. (2) *by reason of political office* — as if one accompanies a Papist prince or lord to mass and Papist processions, he may do this, provided he does not by that reason approve idolatry, or in his own religion dissemble anything to gratify the prince, or simulate in Papist superstition, does not prostrate before the Papist idol, does not beat his breast, does not invoke saints, does not cross himself with the sign, does not by any other reason exhibit devotion or any collusion, but stands only as a *spectator*, looking not at these sacred rites but at his lord, whom the political duty of accompanying demands.**

**Great caution** is needed here, however, lest we seem to *collude* with adversaries. Therefore from their gestures we must abstain: we must not fall on our knees, not beat the breast, not do as the Papists do while the ministering is happening, but rather by whatever signs openly declare our dissent — although this cult of adversaries with laughter, or by some other public sign of contempt, is not to be received.

In this way *Naaman the Syrian* obtained that he might accompany his king to the temple of Rimmon, in which the King indeed adored his idol, but *Naaman* was doing merely the political office of leading him (2 Kgs 5:18).

In these cases external cult of a false-worship is not to be judged as endangering the conscience — provided (i) it is done as a spectator alone; (ii) it is not done against the offense of the weak brother. For even things per se lawful are to be intermitted, if with scandal they cannot be used (1 Cor 8:13). Just so *the Elector and Protestant princes at Augsburg in 1530 refused to accompany Emperor Charles V to the mass and processions of the Feast of Corpus Christi*, because they perceived, in the fasting of the monks, given work, this ministry was demanded from them not merely to render some political office to the Emperor, but that by their presence they might stabilize those Papist abominations — which was not permissible to them, since they wished the confession of the Protestants to be opposed to those abominations (see Coelestin in *Historia Comitiorum August. 1530*, Cent. 2 pt. 1 fol. 92).

### Case VI. Whether under *urgent necessity* one may use the sacred rites of heretics or infidels

**Respondeo.** By *sacred rites* here we understand the Word and sacraments. When we can have these in the true Church without impediment, no one ought to be so rash as to seek them among heretics. But if it happens that one lives among them, and either by reason of office, or on account of some other urgent necessity, cannot altogether depart from them, then what needs to be done must be considered:

**As regards the Word** — since among heretics it is corrupted, rightly do they act who know this, and altogether abstain from hearing of it, since the Word corrupted by human glosses is not the Word of God, but the tradition of men. As the *Pharisees* indeed had the Word of God — for they read Moses and the Prophets in synagogues on the sabbath (Acts 15:21) — yet since they perverted Scripture with their vitiated interpretations, Christ said of them: *they transgress the mandate of God for the tradition of men* (Matt 15:3).

If, however, someone is so confirmed in true faith that without peril of being led astray he can, let him hear, that he may learn to distinguish light from darkness and truth from falsehood — for sometimes it is better that we betake ourselves to the heretics' camp, not as *deserters* but as *scouts*.

**As regards sacraments** — these are of two kinds: *initiation*, and *confirmation*. The **sacrament of initiation** is baptism, which from them is neither to be sought nor received who *pervert the substance of it* — which the Arians do, denying three persons in one divine essence; since Christ commands us to baptize *in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit* (Matt 28:19), while they baptize in the true God, in Jesus Christ savior and creator, and in the Holy Spirit servant of each — as Jerome testifies against the Luciferians, and Athanasius (*Oratio* 3 against the Arians).

Even if they retain the most usual words of institution, the sound of the words is not to be attended (since we ascribe no magical force to them), but rather the true sense which Christ intended in the institution of baptism. In the assemblies therefore of the Arians who *overturn the article of the Trinity*, there is no true baptism; therefore those who have received baptism among them are to be held as unbaptized.

Whence Damascene wrote (*De fide orth.* iv, c. 9): *those who are not baptized in the most sacred Trinity, ought to be rebaptized.* On which account the Paulianists once were rebaptized, since in the assemblies of the Samosatenians denying the article of the Trinity they had been baptized — as is a canon in the *Council of Nicaea* n. 10 and in the fourth *Council of Arelate* n. 8.

**But** if in some orthodox church a *hidden Arian* is minister, he can nonetheless baptize rightly, notwithstanding his own heresy; nor is his ministry to be shrunk from in this kind of case, because *sacraments do not depend on the intention of the minister*, nor is baptism the gift of the minister but of the Church, which if it *thinks rightly* about the articles of faith, and its prayers over the one baptized joins, one need not doubt of the true baptism — especially since not the minister here but *Christ* principally baptizes. Whence the maxim of theology: *sacraments are goods common to the whole Church*.

**In the assemblies of the Papists there is still a true baptism**, by the singular providence of God, lest under such the darkest cover of papacy all should perish, but at least the infants departing at once after baptism from here might be saved. For though certain human inventions have been added to baptism (like chrisma and their exorcisms and superstitions — *salt, oil, chrisma, cera, chrismale, saliva, spittle — ignorant of the truth of baptism*), yet the baptismal water is not polluted, since in itself it is pure, as a creature of God, and divinely ordained for this end, that it cleanse those who are washed in it in Baptism (Eph 5:26) — whence it is called *the laver of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit* (Tit 3:5). Since therefore in Papacy the substance of baptism is retained integral — namely that the baptized are to be baptized in the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — no one ought to doubt of the true baptism, though the ministry has been variously corrupted, provided the words of institution are pronounced according to Christ's institution.

**The sacrament of the Eucharist** — this is not so necessary to salvation as baptism. Therefore it is to be received neither from Papists nor from Calvinists: these have no true eucharist, since they *pervert the substance* of this sacrament — the Papists by removing bread and wine, the Calvinists by removing Christ's body and blood; nay, in Papacy from this sacrament a *sacrifice* is made, and another substantial part, namely *the dominical cup*, is entirely denied to the laity, which does not agree with the substance of the sacrament as instituted by Christ.

Better therefore to abstain from the use of the Eucharist among Papists and Calvinists than against Christ's institution to use it — for here has place that saying of Augustine: *thou hast erred, and thou hast eaten*. And as I said, the use of the sacrament is a *note of confession and of doctrine*; who therefore does not truly acknowledge the doctrine of that Church, in which he wishes to use the sacrament, cannot with safe conscience use the sacrament in that Church.

### Case VII. Whether one may use *private ministry* — when among enemies of true religion the observance of religion is prevented — using a private minister

**Respondeo.** *Private ministry* is called that when the paterfamilias in his own house, for himself and his domestics, uses a pastor called by himself for this end — that to himself and his own in the care of religion he may serve. As often happens, that those who dwell among Papists have in a private house their own *conventicles*, and a pastor called by them for this end — that he may teach the Word of God purely, administer the sacraments legitimately, and copulate marriages and similar offices of the Church.

To this private ministry four *hypotheses* are to be supposed:

**1.** *When the public ministry, even in the place where we dwell, is still uncorrupted, private ministry cannot be used without danger*. It is not permitted that anyone should have his private conventicles for himself: to call ministers of the Word is of the whole Church, whose order and constitution is not to be overturned by that private singularity. Nor is *the public congregation to be forsaken* (Heb 10:25), which is instituted for this — that prayers and sacred rites be conjoined, and with pious hearts serve God. Note also the sighs of David desiring to attend the public sacred rites of the Church (Ps 42:1 ff.); contrariwise ill it fared with *Micah* (Judg 17), who at a time when in the place which the Lord had elected the public ministry stood, in his own house instituted private sacred rites, calling a peculiar Levite for this thing.

**2.** *When ministry indeed in the place where we dwell is corrupted, but in the vicinity without danger we can have purer ministers* — who teach the Word purely, baptize our infants, offer the sacred supper according to the institution of Christ, copulate marriages, visit the sick — then their work is to be used, for no necessity here imposes on us private ministry.

**3.** *When by neighboring ministry without peril we cannot use the neighboring pastor* — from him we must abstain: for charity persuades that we not create for our neighbor some peril which we can avoid.

**4.** *Even though the paterfamilias can privately read the Bible to his own, and by his own strength instruct his family*: yet *privately to baptize his own, absolve from sins, offer the sacred supper, and exercise similar acts of ministry, he cannot*, since all these would happen without a call, and not without scandal and with peril of schisms. On this see Luther's peculiar counsel (Tom. 6, Iena German, fol. 175).

**In this therefore an extreme necessity — when public ministry can in no way be had, nor should anyone without a call seize acts of ministry to himself — it is altogether lawful in conscience to institute private conventicles, to call a private pastor, and to use his ministry.** And he who is so called performs the legitimate office of the Church, and under God's protection can do his office intrepidly.

For Christians without peril of eternal salvation cannot lack the ministry of the Word: for *how shall they believe, if they hear not, and how shall they hear without a preacher?* (Rom 10:14). Nor can they lack the *use of sacraments*, especially of baptism — which, though administered by those who overturn the substance of this sacrament by *heretics* even for a time, was true and legitimate, as we have taught before: yet also is not to be sought from heretics if an *orthodox minister* of the Church can be had, lest we seem to approve *sacred rites from which the pious mind shrinks*, not without scandal to the weaker.

And even though the sacrament of the *Supper* is not so necessary to salvation as baptism — if however some are held by great desire of this sacrament, and from the reasons adduced above are certain that from those who overturn the *substance* of this sacrament they cannot seek it — it is certainly necessary that one *consult by private ministry*.

In this opinion wonderfully confirms us the sentence of Paul, who writes to the Corinthians: *all things are yours* (1 Cor 3:22). If therefore all things are of the Church, doubtless also the constitution of ministry pertains to the Church. Now it cannot be denied that those under the tyranny of a magistrate *alien from true religion* remain the Church — why then should to them be prohibited the care of ministry, if not publicly at least privately to institute it among themselves for their and their own salvation? Since the magistrate impedes what he owes to publicize this ministry, subjects can altogether urge their right and exercise, without any species of rebellion — especially since in the matter of salvation *God must be obeyed more than men*.

Add that no pious man can deny that those who dwell *among Turks or barbarians* — when the barbarian magistrate does not promote public ministry of the divine Word — can institute a private one, lest the care of salvation be impeded. Therefore this also is lawful to those who dwell among Papists or similar enemies of the evangelical truth, and by the magistrate are impeded from the public exercise of their religion. For if in such a class privately to our soul's care it were not lawful, it would follow that our faith and salvation depend on the arbitration of the magistrate, which is altogether absurd. Here we treat not of bodily goods or of fortune, which even the infidel magistrate has subject to his empire, but of the salvation and of things of conscience, in which none but God in heaven has dominion.

Add also examples of those who in a case of necessity among infidels have had their private sacred rites — such as *David*, who at that time when he lived among the Philistines without doubt did not intermit his religion; and *Naaman also from the house of Namur*, and Daniel with a few others converted by him, doubtless privately cared for God's cult, notwithstanding that publicly both ethnics and Jews were exercising another cult (Acts 17:23 ff.).

**Two objections** seem to obtain: (1) that from private ministry *schisms* arise, when in one place a few *particulars*, separating from the community, hold their own peculiar exercises of piety.

*Reply*: These are not *schisms*, since they are recessions not from the Church-malignant but from a legitimate divinely-prescribed separation from the impious and infidels. Nor is it a separation from the Church, since those who use private ministry in a case of necessity are the *particular Church of that place*, joined nonetheless with the universal true and Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world.

Nor is anyone promiscuously to be called a doctor, but he who by other orthodox churches is approved, and about whose sound doctrine there is no doubt.

But even if a great scandal arose from this — it is not to be attributed to the *private ministry* itself but to the *perverse opinions of men*. As it is not permitted to do evil that good may come, so also good is not to be intermitted on account of some evil which is feared. In the public ministry of the *Corinthians* also arose *schisms* on account of the perverse judgments of men, which Paul chastises in the *Prior to the Cor.*, nor is it therefore intermitted; why then should this vice of men hurt private ministry?

**(2)** Some say the orthodox, lest they expose themselves to peril of offending the magistrate, ought to *use the ministry of the adversaries* — just as David once in a case of necessity ate of the show-bread, which was lawful only for other priests to eat (1 Sam 21). By this reasoning, many think the divine precept concerning fleeing idolatry admits a *dispensation*; therefore, so as not to offend the magistrate under whose jurisdiction they live, they think they may attend Mass and other *Papist abominations*, provided that in their heart they contradict them.

But *miserably are they deceived*: **only in ceremonial laws does dispensation have place** — such as the David-and-show-bread case regarding *certain cases* was; but *the moral law never admits dispensation*, for it is the *immoveable and perpetual rule of the divine will*. And to the *moral law* pertains also the *flight from idolatry* and from all abominations, which whoever has acknowledged in his heart, from these also externally in conversation he ought to abstain: otherwise his cult will degenerate into *hypocrisy*, which is contrary to God, who requires not only faith of heart but also confession of mouth from the faithful.

*Nor can any peril be greater than to act against the moral commandments of God*, for the avoidance of which the *corporal and external peril* that threatens from men need not be feared: for God can freely deliver those who cling to him with heart from the hands of enemies. Wherefore Christ wills that we *fear not those who can kill the body, but rather Him who can destroy both body and soul in hell* (Luke 12:5).

### Case IX. Whether the pious can with good conscience live and dwell among enemies of true religion, and by reason of his vocation, which he had from God, refuse to change place, than by living with doubting conscience among them

**Respondeo.** For *nothing is to be done in whatsoever kind of things with doubting conscience*, as gathered from Rom 14:23. But since many make for themselves a scruple in conscience where there is no need, some information in this question is required.

To be known therefore it is, that every Christian lives as it were a *twin life* in this world: (1) *the spiritual*, in which he is called a Christian, and consists in faith, hearing the Word, use of sacraments, and similar parts of divine cult. As regards this life, necessary is *separation of the faithful from the infidels*, of orthodox from heretics: for many admonitions of Paul apply — *what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?* (2 Cor 6:14); *be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers* (2 Cor 6:14); *and Rev 18* — *lest ye be partakers of her sins*, etc. (2) *the political life*, according to which men are, who negotiate, dominate, minister, eat, drink, and do similar things, which pertains to human conversation.

**As regards this life** — one cannot always abstain from conversation with enemies of true religion; otherwise one would have to *depart from the world* (1 Cor 5:10). For *cohabitation is not of light in the darkness of the people*, but of all men dispersed through the world, from which God gathers to himself his Church, in which alone He is acknowledged and worshipped, whose members are not found in one certain place, but through the entire world are dispersed. And of that dispersion *Christ rules in his own kingdom* from sea to sea, even *in the midst of enemies*. Nor does he permit that his people always live among the faithful, but many by reason of their vocation are forced to live among enemies of faith — such as merchants, soldiers, students, and the like, and those also who cannot depart from the paternal seats of their goods.

*In all these, political conversation with enemies of truth is not prohibited.* Therefore Paul (1 Cor 7:12–13) does not command spouses of disparate religion to separate, but *to cohabit*, because *the unfaithful man is sanctified by the faithful wife* — and many serve masters alien from true faith, who therefore need not desert their station: as *in the vocation, in which one is called, so let him remain* (1 Cor 7:20). *Jacob* served in the house of Laban the *idolater* twenty years (Gen 31:41); *Joseph* in the house of Potiphar the Egyptian (Gen 39:4); *Moses* in the house of the Ethiopian priest Jethro (Exod 3); *Daniel* also at the court of *Assyrians* (Dan 1); and Christ himself had his home *among the Capernaites* (Matt 4:13), and with the Pharisees also ate. These *examples of Christ's* show what is lawful in this kind of thing.

But since it is most true that *he who touches pitch shall be defiled thereby* (Sir 13:1), and *he who has fellowship with the proud shall put on pride* — certain cautions are needed if we would preserve a *pure conscience* while dwelling among them:

**1.** *If one who has enemies for cohabitation cannot change his own condition of things*, let him make himself simple and of pure orthodox faith. For consortium with the wicked is dangerous, and often draws to the worse part. Therefore one who among people of pure religion can live, should choose this life more, and by this name congratulate himself: for known is the complaint of David in Ps 120:5: *woe is me, that I sojourn in Meshech, that I dwell in the tents of Kedar!*

**2.** *If one, things not permitting otherwise, is forced to dwell among enemies of truth, let him not imitate their conversations for foreign persons*, but though it is lawful to eat and negotiate with them, let him not do so, but only insofar as necessity and humanity in common life demands. So Christ went to the meals of the Pharisees, but not except when invited.

**3.** *Above all it is to be avoided that in any way with the enemies in religion we consent*, neither by words nor by acts approving their errors — but rather contradicting, when opportunity is given. If we cannot get away without offense, and some *collusion* is sought, let us depart rather from them even bodily, than that we consent to that base hypocrisy. So Christ, even while dining with them, reproved the doctrine and morals of the Pharisees (Luke 14). And it belongs to every Christian *always to be prepared to give a reason for his hope which is in him* (1 Pet 3:15).

**4.** *That we not attend their sacred rites, especially the sacraments* which are the highest matters of religion, and by which we abhor those to whom the sacrament is common. In the vicinity therefore, if it can be done, let him consult for himself and his own about sacred rites, or be content with private exercises of piety — of which more in the preceding.

*Nor are godfathers of Papists to be admitted*, nor should their acts in the sponsorship of baptism be sought — beyond the many other causes of which we spoke in another place; and especially on account of the scandal of the weak brother and species of collusion.

**5.** *No one may become an instrument for propagating false religion*: not as an *amanuensis*, not as a *tabellarius* or *notary* in the cause of religion against confessors of the Gospel; nor in any other way let him promote the *impiety of enemies* — rather let him renounce his office and betake himself to another, though not without loss of his fortune, than to sell his soul to the perpetual dispensation of impiety.

By this reasoning therefore is made a *separation and departure from the enemies of truth in a certain manner*, as *Abraham from Chaldea*, and *Lot from the Sodomites*, and *Jacob from Laban*, went out — the sort of case in which without peril of the soul we can no longer live among them. And in another manner, when we without detriment to religion truly among them stand and dwell, only *approving their impiety in no way*.

— ❦ —

## Chapter VII. On Cases of Conscience Concerning Prayer

*De casibus conscientiae circa orationem.*

Since the chief part of religion is *prayer*, before all things solicitous is the mind of the pious about it — for prayer is the *breath of the soul*, by which we lift up our hearts to God and confess him the fountain of all good. Nor is there any part of the divine cult in which superstition and error creep more easily. Wherefore we shall now propose in order those cases which most often torment consciences.

### Case I. What ought to be attended to in prayer, that our petition may be heard by God

**Respondeo.** Here are to be considered the *conditions of prayer* and of the *one who prays*.

The **conditions of prayer** are three.

**1.** *That it be a due prayer* — that is, directed to the sole God, so that from him alone we ask *all good, and every perfect gift* which comes down from the Father of lights (Jas 1:17). For he alone wills to hear the prayers pouring forth from the heart, and knows how to aid; whereas prayers directed to the saints are *undue*, of which further below.

**2.** *That it be not vain and rash* — for useless and illicit things are not to be sought from God. So the mother of the sons of Zebedee (Matt 20:20), from ambition, asked something for her sons in the kingdom of Christ, which she thought earthly, and received a rebuff. The necessity of things is either of *spiritual things* — such as concern eternal salvation: remission of sins, faith, patience, perseverance in the good, and eternal life itself — or of *bodily things* which pertain to the necessity of this common life: goods of body, of soul, of fortune — and are all comprehended under the fourth petition of the Lord's Prayer in the words *daily bread*.

**3.** *That it be seemly* — such as concerns the glory of God's name and the increase of his kingdom; and which consists *not in multitude of words nor in ornament of words and sentences*, in which for the most part as much verbal ornament accedes so much devotion recedes — but is brief and devout, such as Christ commended when he taught us in praying *not to be many-worded, as the heathen* (Matt 6:7). And Sirach: *let not thy prayer be repetitious* (Sir 7:15). *Repeat the verse*: let it be from the heart, penetrate the ears, be devout.

The **conditions of the one praying** are more.

**1.** *Let him pray in the name of Christ* (John 16:23), by whom we have access to the Father with confidence (Eph 3:12) — *whithersoever the redeemed of Christ are to worship, they are commanded to look to the propitiatory* which is Christ.

**2.** *Let him pray in true faith*, and certain hope of hearing, which Christ has promised. For *not omitting sin* — since no man is *just upon earth, who does good and sins not* (Eccl 7:20) — yet especially from *singular sins*, which wound conscience, we should be strangers when praying; from some of which Scripture names, and by these we may judge of the rest: as **violence and cruelty**, of which the Lord speaks (Isa 1:15): *when ye extend your hands, I will avert mine eyes from you: and when ye multiply orations, I will not hear: your hands are full of blood.* **Unmercifulness**, of which Solomon (Prov 21:13): *he that stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he shall cry, and shall not be heard*. **Inveterate hatred** and rancor of soul against the neighbor, of which Paul (1 Tim 2:8): *I will therefore that men pray everywhere, lifting up holy hands, without wrath*. And Christ (Matt 5:23–24): *if thou bring thy gift to the altar, and there rememberest that thy brother hath ought against thee, leave there thy gift before the altar, and go, first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift*. **Pride**, of which Peter (1 Pet 5:5): *God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble*. **Distrust**, of which Paul when he wills us to pray *without doubting* (1 Tim 2:8), and James (1:6): *let him ask in faith, nothing wavering*. From these and similar delicts the one praying should be a stranger.

**3.** *Let him prepare himself well for prayer* — for he enters into the sight of God, who does not admit anything unclean. Whence David says (Ps 108:8): *My heart is prepared, O God, my heart is prepared: I will sing and I will speak a Psalm*. This preparation requires four things: (i) that the one about to pray unburden his mind of all carnal cares and cogitations — for this is *to pour out one's heart before the Lord* (Lam 2:19); (ii) that with reverence full of the divinity he lift up his heart to God, as David: *unto thee, O Lord, do I lift up my soul* (Ps 25:1); (iii) that he weigh with himself, and premeditate, what he means to propose to God — that admonition of Sirach (5:1): *be not hasty in thy speech, nor slow with thy soul to bring forth aught before God*; (iv) that before he prays he shake out his life, and pray with penitence, as David *first washed his hands in innocence, before he encircled the altar of the Lord* (Ps 26:6).

For since *in many things we slip all* (Jas 3:2), and no one knows all his delicts, the work is worth the effort before all things to seek *remission of sins* — which, obtained, we may more confidently pour out our necessities into the bosom of God. Wherefore also *contritionem* of heart the Lord promised to his people (Isa 66:2). Hither pertains a humble mind and *broken heart, which God despises not* (Ps 51:19) — the manner of Daniel and Ezra praying for their people, first seeking remission of all their sins (Dan 9:5, Sir 39:6).

**4.** *Let him pray not coldly but fervently* — especially in graver perils, such were Christ's prayers in the garden (Matt 26:39). And the rule of Christians is *fervent in spirit* (Rom 12:11). Which fervor is excited by temperance of victual — wherefore the ancients, that they might be more alert to prayer (especially the public), used to prescribe *fastings*, as by the example of the Israelites (Judg 20:26) and Davidic (Ps 35:13).

**5.** *Let him pray instantly*, or as Paul speaks, *unceasingly* (1 Thess 5:17) — for God does not immediately according to our nod, so that he must be urged and importuned, that by this reasoning even God may be moved to have mercy (as Christ taught in the parable of the judge and widow, Luke 18:1ff.).

**6.** *Let him pray with desire and appetite of the things to be sought*, as Hanna (1 Sam 1) in her prayers said: *I pour forth the desire of my soul before the Lord*. And to those who so pray, sighs — even without utterance — take the place of prayers, which is clear from the example of Moses (Exod 14:15).

**7.** *Let him pray for spiritual things without condition*, since they can never hurt us; but for corporal things with the condition of the divine will, since sometimes they may be obscure to us — therefore to be committed to the will of God, who knows omnimode what profits us. In this genus is the example of David (2 Sam 15:26 following) — *if I have found favor in thine eyes, let him bring me back*.

*In these modes* if prayers are instituted, they are pious and pleasing, as, so to speak, dictated to God from a holy mind.

### Case II. Whether the Papists are rightly called *invocators of saints*

**Respondeo.** Not here simply is the question of the saints even yet alive, whether they can intercede for us before God — nay, whether they ought to. For this is enjoined by the Apostle James: *pray for one another, that ye may be saved* (Jas 5:16). So Paul asks the Ephesians (Eph 6:18); and one from another this kind of intercession before God may be sought, as Paul from the Ephesians. Nor of the saints of the Old Testament, whom Paul in Heb 11 refers as a *catalogue of saints*, whose beatitude is certain, so that also in the Papacy the proverb has been familiar: *many relics are collected, of which today all remembrance is lost*.

Nor of *fabulous saints*, or such as are doubtful whether they lived thus at all — such are Christopher, Lotobicus, whom they call Godfather, Catharina, Georgius — whom the Papists count among the saints. Some are more ancient, whose true or feigned virtues and acts are proposed in the Church, preached and commended, so that if all things are true, the whole of the Church, seeking the truth by works and *strenuously contending for the truth*, may retain unbroken the immortal faith.

The **imitation of the saints** is enjoined (Heb 13:7): *remember them who have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the Word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation*. And (Heb 6:12): *be followers of them, who through faith and patience inherit the promises*.

Since the works of the saints are of three kinds — precepts, prohibited, and heroic — to be known it is that *imitation is to be instituted only according to the first kind*, in which the saints and we alike are set. Not in the second — for the sins of the saints are not for imitation but *for consolation*, as Ambrose said. Nor of the third — for heroic acts are to be imitated not by us but by those who have a peculiar vocation from God to such things. In this manner the *saints departed* are sufficiently honored by us.

But the Papists, not content with this, moreover add to the cult *invocation of saints*, whom in the *Psalter* also they hail as *lord of heaven and earth*, and to whom things are attributed which cannot be adorned except by fable, and in the Papacy such invocation is proposed and to be believed.

*This distinction is contrary to Scripture* (Rom 1:4 and 3:18), where invocation is *proper to God*, since faith must be had of him who is thence to be invoked. It is *rejected by the most learned of the Papists themselves*, Cajetan, L. Vives, and others. It is *Nestorian*, to divide Christ into a mediator only quoad naturam, quoad naturam humanam. It is *Judaical*, servitude not only to men but even not enough to God (Deut 32:34) — *ye shall serve the God of your fathers* (Mal 3:14), *ye shall serve Christ* (Col 3:24), *serving the Lord Jesus Christ* (Rom 12:11).

The Papists — not content with mere invocation, further add the cult of *hyperdulia* of Mary and other cults, which they say — three causes: (1) on account of our indigence, as Alexander of Hales speaks, whom we should imitate in this discipline, so that at least by their merits we may attain to what by ours we cannot; (2) on account of *the glory of the saints themselves*, whom they call ministers and dispensers of all goods, both spiritual and corporal, as *Gabriel Biel* has it (on *Canon of the Mass*, lection 24); (3) on account of the *reverence of God*.

Hence Lombard writes (iv, dist. 45): *the saints intercede for us with God, and by merit — while by their merit they aid us — obtain what we desire.* Therefore we ask, that they intercede for us, that is, that their merits may suffice for us. And the Council of Trent (Sess. 25) decrees that the saints are to be invoked with confidence, humbly fleeing to their aid.

They teach also, of the *justice of God*, an appeal is to be made to the *forum of the mercy of Mary*, as Bernardinus has it in his *Marial*. And thus all confidence due to God alone is transferred to Mary suppliantly in the *Psalter of Mary*.

> *Notable is the deceit which he plainly proposes.* In the first place stands the ancient sinner, turning his face to the Blessed Virgin with this address: *I beg thee, O pious Virgin, defend me now, Mary. From one side, Mary denudingly begins to address Christ her Son, since she is his mother, mercy I entreat, deigning to point out the sinner. From the other side, Christ shows his wounds to the Father in these words: See the wounds, Father, do that which my mother asks; in the highest constituted the heavenly Father concludes: Whatever thou askest, I will grant, Son, I will deny thee nothing.* [See Scripture pertaining to *D. Gerhard*, p. 713 tom. 5.]

They teach that *by the help of the saints*, prayer is better and more happily brought before God, as Bellarmine has it (i, *De sanctorum beatitudine*, c. 10) — they call the saints ministers and *dispensers* of any goods whatsoever, both spiritual and corporal, as *Gabr. Biel* holds (*super canonem Missae*, sect. 4, lect. 3).

To *singular provinces and cities, animals, and orders* also, singular saints are pre-set — whom not only by prayers but also by *oblations, donaries, vows, dedications of temples, and similar acts*, they religiously worship. All these things in the Papacy are taught in use, and are propounded as things to be believed.

> [To the *Germans* Georgius, to the *Spanish* Jacobus, to the *Gauls* Dionysius, to the *Bulgarians* Ludovicus, to the *Milanese* Ambrosius they set forth. To the *Turchi Sylvanus*, glory to the sows and lambs, to *Gauls of geese*, of sheep Vindelinus, of hogs Antony, of the stables of horses Catherine, of shepherds Lucas — *for the pest is prayed to Sebastian*, for the teeth Apollonia, for the eyes Otilia, for the stone Libanius, for epilepsy Valentine.]

But of all sorts they are, which cannot with safe piety and conscience be admitted — for as fixed it is that saints must be held *neither as mediators, nor as intercessors, nor as helpers, nor by whatsoever other name are they to be invoked* — but whosoever does this, is stained with the crime of *idolatry*, to be settled.

**First, it is clear from the mouth of Christ**: *in vain do they worship God with the mandates of men* (Matt 15:9). And the mandates of men are which have no certain Word. And it is confessed by all Papists, that no dogma is to be received in the Church which does not have foundation in Scripture (Matt 15:13): *every plantation, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up* — says the Savior (Matt 15:13). And by this same foundation the Samaritan invocation was rejected, though of no time prescription nor patristic authority destitute — because it was *destitute of God's Word*.

*God also in the Law willed idolaters to be punished, because they adored what he himself did not prescribe* (Deut 17:3, 4). The Papists confess, no mandate exists nor exemplum in sacred writings that this be commanded. Right writes Georgius Casander (*Preface*). *Occhus*, in his *Enchiridion*, does not permit *worship of saints* — reasons he adds why in Scripture invocation of saints was not prescribed in the OT: because *the people were otherwise prone to idolatry, and the Fathers were still in Limbo and not blessed*, as (Isa 63:16): *Abraham knew us not, and Israel was ignorant of us* — under the Gospel therefore was not commanded, lest gentiles converted think that they were again introduced to the cult of the ancients; and *for old custom* saints, not as *patrons* but as *gods* to be adored, as when the Lycaonians wanted to sacrifice to Paul and Barnabas. Moreover, if the Apostles and Evangelists had taught it, they would surely have prescribed it. But Paul commands the contrary (Eph 6:18, Heb 4:16).

Add, that *the saints themselves this honor detest*, as *Bartholomew* the angel and *John* the Apostle admit (Rev 22:9): *see that thou do it not, worship God*.
