**Then, in the sermon, a right disposition of heart is necessary.**

For this is required: (i) that the heart be *discerning*, that is, that the Word be heard *with judgment*.

This judgment turns either about the *preacher* himself or about the *Word*.

*In the preacher* many are the *imperfections, weaknesses, and defects*, both in morals and in gestures and external gifts. These are to be borne patiently, and one is to attend *not so much who speaks as what is said*. Although (as *Gregory* says in Hom. 12): *if the life of the preacher is contemned, the preaching is condemned*, yet the *efficacy of the Word does not depend on the life of the teacher*: for the Holy Spirit, even through impure canals, sends his own gifts, as he taught even through Judas.

*The gifts of the doctors also* are to be attended, that we not, if some abound with greater ones, look down on the ministry of others: for *the virtue of God is perfected in weakness* (2 Cor 12:9); *diversities of gifts there are, yet the same Spirit* (1 Cor 12:4). Whence *Paul* reprehends the *Corinthians*, that *by reason of the diversity of gifts they had made schisms among their teachers, so that one named Peter, another Apollos, another Paul*: with what accusation he objects to them (1 Cor 1:5,6): *is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?* — *what is Apollo, what is Paul, but ministers, through whom ye have believed, and to each God gave as he willed* (1 Cor 3:4,5). Wherefore to a doctor whom God has enriched with such riches of gifts, when in others we see they are lesser, we ought not on that account abhor his doctrine, but cogitate: *in a great house are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay* (2 Tim 2:20). Here also let that Apostle be heard: *judge ye yourselves what I say* (1 Cor 10:15).

*The Word of the doctor also* the auditor should judge, according to what the Apostle said: *judge ye what I say* (1 Cor 10:15). For the Apostle does not want us to be *credulous to every spirit, but to try the spirits, whether they be of God* (1 John 4:1). For at length come *tempests*, who care for no religion, hold sound doctrine for jest — so far from converting it into juice and blood — as was **Felix**, who *when Paul discussed of faith, of righteousness, of chastity, of the judgment to come, being terrified answered: go thy way, in a fit time I will call for thee* (Acts 24:25).

That this judgment may be rightly instituted, let there be laid down *for foundation the Word of God*, to which as to the *Lydian stone* the words of the one speaking should be compared, as the *Beroeans* did (Acts 17:11). So the Lord commanded the people to receive the law from the mouth of the priest (Mal 2:7). *To the law then, that is, to the Word of God, the words of the preacher are to be examined.*

**(2)** *Let not this judgment flow from carnal affection, but be instituted in the fear of the Lord, in study of truth and desire of learning* — for *spiritual are they who discern all things* (1 Cor 2:15).

**(3)** *Let it make a right application* of the things which are said, selecting namely those things which any one knows to be most necessary for himself. For every auditor ought to judge that *the business is with him*: if he thinks only that what is said pertains to others, in vain will he hear, and without judgment.

**(ii)** For the *right disposition of the heart* in hearing there is required — *let it not be too lax*, in which what is heard soon flows out, such a heart as is compared by Christ *to the ground lying by the way, in which the seed of the divine Word is either trampled by feet, or by the devil, before it can take root, is taken away* (Luke 8:5).

*Such a heart is:*

**(1)** *Of the doubting*, who are borne about by every wind of doctrine, call in doubt all they hear, nowhere stand safely, and by this reason always *learning* but *never coming to the knowledge of the truth*. Just as *Festus* thought *Paul* mad when he was disputing about the vocation of the gentiles to the Church (Acts 26:24). To these should be inculcated the Apostolic saying: *let us not be little children, wavering and carried about with every wind of doctrine* (Eph 4:14).

**(2)** *Of those sordid in sins*, who by long use have drawn upon themselves the habit of sin. Whatever thou shalt say to these, thou speakest to deaf ears; they indeed shudder when they hear of the pains of sins and the examples of those who suffered them, but quickly the passing wrath of God — since it is servile — scarce turns them from the doctor. To the old genius they return: such was *Felix*, who with his wife *Drusilla* was hearing *Paul* speaking about faith in Christ, about righteousness, chastity, the judgment to come, being terrified answered, *go thy way, in a fit time I will call for thee* (Acts 24:25). Similar are these to the sick who flee the physician's summons before they are bound. These should be roused from the slumber of sins by continued acclamations, and often the wrath of God should be set before their eyes — how great is the peril with which they familiarize themselves in sins should be crebrously inculcated, according to *Paul's* admonition (2 Tim 4:2): *preach the Word, be instant in season, out of season, reprove, entreat, rebuke in all patience and doctrine*.

**(3)** *Of the wanton* (*lascivientium*), who attend not what is said by the preacher, but only how pompously in words and gestures he proposes his matter — these lick the *bark* of sermons, scarcely attaining to the marrow. Such were those of whom the Lord speaks (Isa 29:30): *lo, ye have taken my words in your mouth, and they hear thy words, but do them not*. To these should be opposed the custom of the Apostle *Paul*, of which he himself writes (1 Cor 2:4): *my speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power*; and to memory should be recalled the other saying (1 Cor 4:20): *the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power*. To this class belong also those who *in weariness of mind hear the Word, or altogether close their eyes during teaching*; these sit with closed ears and hearts, perceiving nothing of the things said, because they seem to them *trite and obsolete*. *Demosthenes* upbraided the Athenian people that they wanted to hear him when he spoke about *the ass's shadow*, but did not want to hear him disputing about the salvation of Greece. Much more reprehensible is this in Christians, who come to the hearing of the Word not into some theater, nor to see a play, but into the house of God, and in sight of the saints, of angels, sit to hear about the salvation of their own soul. These therefore from the sleep of their negligence are to be excited by that saying of Christ: *he who has ears to hear, let him hear* (Luke 8:8), and by the Apostle Paul (Eph 5:14): *awake, thou that sleepest, and Christ shall give thee light*.

**(4)** *Of the temporary*, who receive the Word with joy for a time only — while affairs are prosperous — but when the heat of persecution and perils breaks in, they wither, and *the doctrine once received they no longer profess*, since they fear peril. Therefore they are called *temporary*, because they serve the *time*, and for a light cause they change religion. Such were the Capernaites, who sought Christ because from the *five loaves* he had satisfied them, but shortly after they left his sermons (John 6:26,66). Among the Hierosolymitans also there were some, of whom John (12:42) testifies: *many of the rulers believed in him, but on account of the Pharisees they did not confess, lest they should be cast out of the synagogue*. *Such were the Galatians*, of whom *Paul* testifies that *if it were possible, they would have plucked out their own eyes and given them to him* (Gal 4:15) — and yet he complains of them, that *deceived they should not obey the truth* (Gal 5:7). To these should be inculcated that saying of the Apostle: *it hath been given us by Christ, not only that we should believe, but also that we should suffer for him* (Phil 1:29); and that *then only is he a true participant of Christ, who keeps the beginning firm to the end* (Heb 3:14).

**(5)** *Of the indurate* (*induratorum*), who in sins are hardened, nor have they a purpose of amending their life. Whatever thou shalt say to these about heaven or hell, thou tellest to a deaf tablet. As therefore the rain falling on a rock somewhat wets it outwardly, but because it does not penetrate cannot irrigate — so these, however affected by moving sermons, are not touched to the heart, which the devil occupies, *who blinds the minds of unbelievers, that the illumined glory of Christ's gospel should not shine on them* (2 Cor 4:4). Such were the *hearers of Jeremiah*, of whom he complains (Jer 5:3): *they did not grieve; thou hast crushed them, and they refused to receive discipline; they hardened their faces*; and (Jer 6:10): *to whom shall I speak, whom shall I obtestate, that he may hear? Lo, uncircumcised are their ears, they cannot hear, the Word of God is made unto them a reproach, and they receive it not*. So *Zechariah* complains of his hearers (Zech 7:11): *they refused to attend and turned away the shoulder, retreating, and made their ears heavy that they might not hear*. Such were the hearers of *Stephen*, who *were cut in their hearts, and gnashed with their teeth against him* (Acts 7:54).

*The requisites of the indurate*, by which they are recognized, are these: (a) *contumacy*, when they are led by no sense of divine threatenings (John 12:40; Eph 4:18); (b) *pain-less-ness* (*ἀπαλγή*), when they feel no longer any pain of the wounded conscience — whence they are called *ἀπηλγηκότες* (Eph 4:19); (c) *spirit of stupor* (*κατάνυξις*, Rom 11:8), which *Isaiah* names *spirit of drowsiness* (Isa 29:10), by which not only is the judgment of conscience repelled and petulantly overthrown, but also the man partly burns with hatred against the well-admonishing, partly suffers the conflict of thoughts mutually accusing and defending themselves; (d) they are called *reprobate* (*ἀδόκιμοι*) (2 Tim 3:8) — that is, by the just judgment of God deprived of all faculty of judging, so that they cannot discern what is of their own use. Paul calls them *evil men and seducers* (2 Tim 3:13), *who proceed to worse, deceiving and being deceived*. There accedes finally contradiction and blasphemy of the things said, which the indurate not only do not receive with meekness, but contemn — nor do they merely contemn, but with blaspheming mouth speak against them, as if not true, in the way that the *Pharisees* spoke against Christ: *thou bearest witness of thyself, thy testimony is not true* (John 8:13). And certain indurate *Jews in the synagogue of Ephesus were speaking evil of the way of the Lord before the multitude* (Acts 19:9); others in the synagogue of Antioch *contradicted Paul and blasphemed* (Acts 13:45). To these indurate should be seriously inculcated that of the Apostle: *according to thy hardness and impenitent heart, thou treasurest up wrath unto thyself in the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God* (Rom 2:5).

Let them cogitate that the *Word of God is efficacious, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit* (Heb 4:12) — no wonder therefore if it *cut the heart* and *wound sinners* not without pain, but with great fruit to themselves — if they patiently admit this sword.

**(iii)** *Let not the heart of the auditor be too thorny*, in which the Word once heard is suffocated before it either takes root or brings forth fruit — such a heart as Christ compares to the field beset with thorns and briars (Luke 8:7).

*Such a heart is:*

**(1)** *Of the anxious* (*anxiorum*), who are too much implicated with the solicitudes of this age, attending only to matters, occupied about carnal things — whence they are neither seriously solicitous about the things of the soul, nor can be far from domestic cares during the sermon. For as *Bernard* speaks: *by pursuit of spiritual meditations, our heart is as it were agglutinated to earthly things, so that with serious study it cannot be raised to the heavenly and celestial* (Sermon 3 *In quadragesima*). Such was the heart of that *rich man* (Luke 12:19) who said to his soul: *thou hast much goods for many years, rest, eat, drink, be merry* — but God said to him, *fool, this night thy soul is required of thee, and whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?* Let there be opposed to these vain cares the voice of Christ: *seek ye first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you* (Matt 6:33); and Paul's: *the Lord is at hand, be careful for nothing* (Phil 4:5).

**(2)** *Of the avaricious* (*avarorum*), who so pant after the riches of this age, that they cannot without hurt to themselves listen well to the Word: for they, by *many useless and noxious desires which drown men in destruction and perdition* (1 Tim 6:9). *They savor of earthly things, their god is the belly, their end is destruction* (Phil 3:19). For on account of accumulating riches they spurn the great supper (Luke 14:18) and royal nuptials (Matt 22:5) — as were the *Pharisees*, who *hearing Christ's parable of the unjust steward, mocked him, for they were covetous* (Luke 16:14). But to this evil there is remedy in Christ's admonition: *take heed and beware of covetousness, for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth* (Luke 12:15) — and the meditation of the instability of all temporal things, which at length must be forsaken, nor can they profit any in the day of wrath (Zeph 1:18; Ezek 7:19). Therefore safe is it in this part to follow David's counsel: *if riches abound, set not your heart on them* (Ps 62:10).

**(3)** *Of the voluptuous* (*voluptuosorum*), who are preoccupied with desires of the flesh, in whose fulfilment they locate the highest good. Hence it is no wonder that they hear the Word without fruit. For their heart is too soft — indeed also full of chinks — hither and thither it lets everything through. The voluptuousness of the flesh implicates the heart and depresses pious cogitations in it, so that they think *nothing more pleasant or desirable than to indulge the genius and to fulfil the desire of the flesh*: whence it happens that they hear not the salutary admonitions, contemn salutary precepts, and reject all discipline. Such was the heart of those *impious ones* who *derided the sermons of Christ's advent to judgment* (2 Pet 3:4); who did not believe the resurrection of the dead, saying: *let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die* (1 Cor 15:32; Isa 22:13); who *petulantly contemn the admonitions of the elders* (Wisd 2:12) — in which chapter the *petulance* of these men is at length described.

[*Cicero* (Tusc. Quaest. 5) attributes this epitaph to *Sardanapalus*: *These things I have — what I have eaten, what my libidinous rapture drank; but there lie many, great, and famous things left behind. Clemens* of Alexandria (Strom. 1) so rendered it: *ταῦτ' ἔχω, ὅσσ' ἔφαγον, καὶ ἀφύβρισα, καὶ σὺν ἔρωτι — those things I have which I ate, in which I indulged, and with love.*]

These filths must be purged from the minds of auditors by *serious consideration of the divine judgment*, which touches the impure — for which cause Christ exhorts: *take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be burdened with surfeiting and drunkenness* (Luke 21:34); and Peter: *abstain from carnal desires, which war against the soul* (1 Pet 2:11); and John: *love not the world, nor the things that are in the world. If any love the world, the charity of the Father is not in him: for all that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, and the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not of the Father, but of the world* (1 John 2:15,16).

All these things pertain to the *true disposition* of the mind in auscultation of the Word. For as no seed is of such good nature but that it degenerates, if it falls into ground not rightly disposed — so also the seed of the divine Word by nature incorruptible is nonetheless corrupted, and loses its efficacy, unless the heart in the auditors be rightly disposed.

**Now follows the third thing which is necessarily required in the salutary hearing of the divine Word. After the sermon this concerns the *keeping* of the divine Word: *blessed are they who hear the Word of God and keep it* (Luke 11:28); and with these the Word once heard *fell on good ground* — who *with a good heart hearing the Word, receive it, retain it, and bring forth fruit with patience* (Mark 4:20; Luke 8:15).**

Four here are shown to us as *offices of the auditors after the hearing of the Word*, necessarily to be observed:

**(1)** *To have a good heart* — that is, purged of perverse affections, elevated to God, and well-disposed toward the doctor of the Word, which is done when the auditor is inflamed with love toward God (who feeds him with his Word) and toward the ministers of the Word as *coadjutors of God*, and holds the office of instruction *for highest benefit, with purpose of expressing in his life those things which he heard in the sermon* — for *not the hearers only, but the doers of the Word are required* (Jas 1:22). And since this is not in our powers, let there accede a *serious vow to God*, that he himself seal the Word in our hearts, and give us mind to institute our life according to it.

**(2)** *To receive the Word with meekness*, and to hide it in the heart. In this manner *David* received the Word, as he writes in Psalm 119: he *not only loved it above gold and silver, but also hid it in his heart, that he might not sin against it* (Ps 119:11). Of the *Beroeans* it is also related that they received the Word *with all readiness of mind, and daily searched the Scriptures* (Acts 17:11). *The Thessalonians* received the Word as they heard it, *not as the word of men, but as it truly is, the Word of God* (1 Thess 2:13). *James* also exhorts us that we *receive with meekness the ingrafted Word, which is able to save our souls* (Jas 1:21). Well is it done with those who do this — for these *receive Christ himself*: *whoever receiveth me*, he says, *doth not receive me only, but him that sent me* (John 13:20). And with these the *whole Trinity has its habitation*, as the Lord testifies (John 14:23). Now the Word is received when there is not only faith about the things said, but also a special *application* of the things said is made, as our use demands: if we are sad or tempted, let us apply the consolatory Word to ourselves; if of any thing guilty, let there be applied to us the reproofs — and thus consequently we may judge the things said; thus at length may the Word truly root itself in our hearts. For it is written of the Word that it did not profit those who *did not mix it with faith in the hearing* (Heb 4:2).

**(3)** *To retain the Word received*, that it not soon slip through the ears, but strike root in the heart, until the time of fructification come. For sometimes the Word lies in the heart, as seed in the field, and does not immediately manifest its efficacy — it discloses the same in due time by the Holy Spirit.

To which matter it is useful, that we *ruminate the Word once heard*; for ruminant animals were served both to men for food and to God for sacrifice (Lev 11; Deut 14; Isa 3). This *ruminatio* of the Word is *diligent meditation* of those things which we heard — for this is *to meditate in the law of the Lord day and night*, which is said of the pious in Psalm 1. Then also, *serious examination of our life* is needed, whether it agrees with the things we heard; and if some defect appear, let us maturely think of emendation. Thus did *David* (Ps 119:59): *I thought on my ways, and turned my feet unto thy testimonies*. Hence at length is the Word heard *to us the odor of life* (2 Cor 2:16), that *we may taste and see, how sweet is the Lord to those who fear him* (Ps 34:8).

**(4)** *The Word once received ought to bear fruit* — it should not lie torpid in the hearts of the auditors, but grow up, and by the *fruits of faith* by which it was received, so that we be *doers* and not only *hearers*. Here pertains the *obedience of the pious*, who seek to please God in all things, whose *light shines before men, that they see their good works* (Matt 5:16); who according to *Peter's* admonition *give all diligence to add to their faith virtue, to virtue knowledge, to knowledge abstinence, to abstinence patience, to patience piety, to piety brotherly kindness, to brotherly kindness charity* (2 Pet 1:5,6). This fructification ought to be in *patience*: for those who do the will of the Lord do not always enjoy prosperity, but *judgment begins from the house of God* (1 Pet 4:17). Therefore here is patience necessary, that we *doing the will of God may bear away the promise* (Heb 10:36) — for *to them who love God all things at length work together for good* (Rom 8:28).

*These are the three requirements of the pious man* — *before, in, and after the sermon* — where they are found, there the Word does not lack its fruit, but is *the Word of life*, refreshing the soul, preserving the man in death itself unto life eternal, as the Savior said (John 8:51): *verily, verily, I say unto you, if any keep my Word, he shall not see death for ever*.

### Case III. What is to be done, if someone has a desire to hear the Word, but cannot have the Word itself, and yet is meanwhile anguished in his heart by that of Rom 10:17 — *faith is by hearing*?

**Respondeo.** This desire may be of two kinds. Either it is the *penalty of preceding contempt of the Word*, which God threatened, that *he will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, but of hearing the Word of the Lord, so that they shall be commoved from sea to sea, and from the north to the east, they shall run about seeking the Word of the Lord, and shall not find it* (Amos 8:11,12). And it happens for the most part, that those who felt weariness of the divine Word when it dwelt richly among them, afterward, when it is taken away, seek it with desire — in whom not unfitly those *stings* of *faith by hearing* excite themselves, whereby their heart is *lancinated*.

*Serious penitence therefore is needful*, that they may acknowledge they have deprived themselves of that treasure by their great desert. If then their desire is *serious*, they can meanwhile fill it up by *private reading and meditation*, until God, moved by their penitence and sighs, sends again through the public ministry the rays of his Word to them.

Sometimes indeed the desire happens *by some case, without the man's fault*, who was always a sedulous hearer of the Word — but by a long disease, or by exile, or by prison, or by the violence of enemies, who expelled the doctors of the Gospel, cannot be present at the public preaching of the divine Word. In this very *desire of hearing the Word*, a part of divine cult exists, for by it he conjoins his soul with the multitudes of the faithful who can hear the Word without impediment — just as *David* did (Ps 42:1): *as the hart panteth after the water-brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God*, &c.; *I have poured out my soul, because I wished to pass over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle*, &c.

Meanwhile they ought to be *content with private exercises of piety* — with *reading* and *meditation* of the Word, which in this case is in place of a public preaching. For the *Gospel can be preached even if it is only read* without accession of interpretation; as *Moses* is said to be preached in the synagogues, since he was read on each Sabbath (Acts 15:21). Hence *Chrysostom* (Hom. 9 in Epist. ad Coloss.) exhorts: *procure for yourselves Bibles, medicaments of the soul*, &c.

Nor should any make for himself a scruple from Rom 10. Certain interpretations there are which impede this scruple.

*Clemens Alexandrinus* (Strom. 6) attributes hearing to the mind, from the sentence of *Epicharmus*: *the mind sees, the mind hears; other things are deaf and blind*. According to this interpretation, the sense of the Pauline dictum would be: *from serious meditation of the divine Word comes faith*. Thus the matter would indeed be safe, and no scruple would remain: but the preceding attest that the Apostle speaks of the *hearing of ears*, or of the *action of hearing* — just as Luke says: *when the Word was received by ears, the Lord opened her heart, that she attended to those things that were said by Paul* (Acts 16:14).

*Schwenckfeldius* accepts *Paul's* words about the *internal* hearing, which is immediate from the Holy Spirit; which interpretation indeed would remove the scruple, but is not consonant with the text. For although we concede that internal hearing which is by the Holy Spirit and consists in *assent* to the divine Word is required for faith, yet the Holy Spirit *does not work immediately outside that external hearing which is by ears, but through it* — since so cohere his words: *how shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach except they be sent? — But not all obey the Gospel; for Isaiah says, Lord, who hath believed our report? So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the Word of God*. Where the order is shown by which God promotes salvation of men — namely, through the *ministry of the Word*, which is preached externally and heard by us. As therefore in Isaiah's words *hearing* is put for the *preaching of the Gospel*, so also when *faith is said to be from hearing*, hearing is to be accepted of that preaching which is perceived by ears. So indeed Christ in Luke 8 uses: *the Holy Spirit* works efficacy *through the preaching of the Gospel and the auditum and expended matter*.

Since therefore by this interpretation the scruple is not removed, it is to be said, that *Paul* indeed treats of the *external hearing of the preached Word* — which is the *ordinary* organ of obtaining faith — but the case of necessity is always excepted. For also *the deaf by nature cannot hear the Word*, yet faith cannot be denied to them; for in these God works in another manner, namely, by *reading* the Word: for it has also *witnesses* also *ears*. So also captives can, if they read and meditate on the Word, by these very means obtain, augment, and preserve faith in time of disease, peril, and persecutions.

For the *external hearing* is not a perpetual and absolute necessary medium of obtaining faith: other auditors of the Word all have faith. But in perils and defect of the public ministry the exercises of the Word must be more arduous *than outside peril*, where among many the *plenty of the Word* introduces security, by which faith is lost — whence it does not follow that this external hearing of the Word is absolutely necessary to faith.

### Case IV. What if even the sacred books be forbidden, by whose reading the faithful could feed themselves in this defect of ministry?

**Respondeo.** As has happened frequently in the *Papacy*, where when they expelled orthodox pastors, they also *extorted the Bible from the simpler ones* — whom they wanted to have fed rather with legendary tales than with the food of sacred letters. For thus has *Alfonsus a Castro* (in art. 1 *De vera fide*): *whatever it is of religion, altogether must the reading of sacred letters be forbidden to the universal laity*. The *Censure of the Theological Faculty of Paris* similarly against *Erasmus*, that *the Bible is not a fitting Breviary in the hands of any woman, though a virgin, so that she should not open sacred letters*. And *Bellarmine* writes (lib. 2 *De verbo Dei* c. 15): *the reading of prohibited books* (among which even are also *sacred Bibles* in vulgar tongues) *is required. This has not been so much required for scholars; and though it is prohibited by the ordinary that they should proceed*, *yet it is prohibited that the auditors should be indiscriminately conceded*.

In this state one should not expect *revelations of secret matters, or revelations outside the Word*: but (1) here at last does that *rumination and meditation of the Word previously heard* have its use, of which I spoke above. Then indeed above all in the pious that office of the Holy Spirit shines forth which consists in *suggesting*, of which Christ says (John 14:26): *the Comforter shall suggest to you all things whatsoever I have said unto you* — for then the seed which hitherto lay in the good heart as if dead begins to fructify. Through the Word previously heard therefore the Holy Spirit works faith and consolation in those who *diligently ruminate and meditate the things heard* — which many sick and captive experience. This matter ought to move us to a *diligent and attentive* hearing of the Word, not superficial, while we can still hear it.

**(2)** *Sacred colloquies with others* who also love the Word and fear God — through whose ministry in this case the Holy Spirit is most efficacious, of which matter we have an illustrious example (Acts 18:24 seqq.), where *Apollos*, a certain eloquent man and mighty in the Scriptures, disputed indeed *of Christ* with confidence in the synagogue, but through the colloquies of *Aquila* and *Priscilla* was more diligently informed in this doctrine of Christ. So *Timothy*, from constant conversation with his grandmother and mother, was instructed from the *sacred letters* in his childhood (2 Tim 1:5; 3:14,15). To this *meditation and collation* on the Word of God *David* attributes rooting and increment in faith, with mention of good works, drawing daily fruit from thence, in Psalm 1.

**(3)** *Who are spoiled of the reading and hearing of the Word can console themselves also from Baptism*, in which they were donated with faith. For that is a *good stipulation of the conscience with God* (1 Pet 3:21), and what God there promised us he will not rescind: for *God is faithful, he cannot deny himself* (2 Tim 2:13). Here let there succor the *serious will of God for our salvation*, the *gratuitous donation of the Son*, the *serious calling to the Church*: by the use of which benefits still enjoy those who are deprived of exercise of the Word through the tyranny of men beyond their mind. Therefore he who desires this food, though he cannot have it, let him not doubt, but the grace conferred on him in Baptism, God will seal even in him, mediating the information of the pastors, and as long as he does not resist.

**(4)** *Much can holy prayers do in this matter*, that the Lord may augment faith in us and *perfect the good work* he has begun in us; which God knows how to perform himself, and will perform, though the ordinary means by which the tranquil enjoy be denied by the injury of others. *Whatsoever we shall ask according to his will, he heareth us* (1 John 5:14).

**(5)** *If the pious mind, deprived of the exercise of the Word, cannot yet acquiesce*, let it study that in the interim it may run out elsewhere, that it may be fed with the Word of God — as the *Judaic people*, having left their ordinary doctors, followed *Christ* even into the wilderness; and *Naaman* set out from *Syria* to *Elisha* in *Judea*, by whom he was freed both from corporal and from spiritual leprosy (2 Kgs 5); the *eunuch of Queen Candace* set out from Ethiopia to Jerusalem for divine cult (Acts 8). But if not even this be permitted by the violence of tyrants, then, all things being left, and with some loss of family goods, let him change his domicile. *For better it is to be an abject in the house of God than to dwell in the tabernacles of sinners* (Ps 84:10). It is also better to be deprived of the goods of fortune than of the treasure of the soul, especially since the promise of luculent retribution is made for that loss (Matt 19:29).

### Case V. Whether an auditor, having abandoned his ordinary pastor, may with good conscience seek care for his soul from another?

**Respondeo.** Here we are not treating of those who *travel*, or by reason of their business live among strangers, where they cannot have the plenty of their ordinary pastor. These do not sin, if with strangers they also hear the Word, use the Lord's Supper, and if perchance they fall into disease or some temptation, they use also the consolation, absolution, and similar ministry of other orthodox pastors — for *necessity has no law*. Neither of those who inhabit such a city where exercises of diverse religions are publicly permitted — and forth from the *Papist* religion (to which perhaps from their parents they were addicted) they for just cause become alienated, and repair to some evangelical pastor and use his ministry — these too do not sin: *they are commanded to depart out of Babylon* (Rev 18:4). Nor of those who indeed enjoy an orthodox ministry, but the pastor himself does not deign to serve them with his ministry, envies them a place among auditors, does not admit them to absolution or to the use of the sacraments, without just cause and without preceding legitimate cognition. These, convicted of the injury done to them in their own conscience, do not sin, if the food of the soul which they cannot extort from the reluctant ordinary pastor they seek elsewhere — provided they always have a mind alien from hatred or contempt of their ordinary pastor.

But we treat of those who *litigate with their ordinary pastor in court*, or *for some cause hold a mind more disposed against him* — of these it is asked: *whether with good conscience, neglecting his ministry, they may implore the work of another pastor, hear his sermons only, and seek from him absolution and the Lord's Supper?*

They allege indeed the *greater devotion* of their mind when they use the ministry of foreign pastors. They deny that they can admit with any fruit the work of their pastor, with whom they nurse dissensions: but these are naked pretexts.

We have *reasons* not to be contemned, which ought to move them to lay aside their quarrels and be content with the ministry of their ordinary pastor, that they not commit themselves to strangers.

**(1)** *Scripture first requires this*, in those places where to each bishop or pastor a certain flock is committed — as when *Paul* names the bishops of the Ephesians *whom the Holy Spirit hath appointed* to feed the flock (Acts 20:28); when *Peter* exhorts the presbyters to *feed the flock which is committed to them* (1 Pet 5:2). And in general the *ratio of ecclesiastical ministry* postulates that each pastor not have the care of all men promiscuously, but a certain flock over which he give his work — for by this very thing the *ecclesiastical minister* is distinguished from the Apostles, who were doctors of the whole world constituted by Christ. For which cause also *Paul* sent his disciples away to certain particular churches, *Titus* into *Crete*, &c. Whence rightly we conclude that auditors ought to be *content with their ordinary pastors*, lest they cast them into the *crimen ἑτεροδιδασκαλίας*.

**(2)** *The auditors also have the precept, that they render obedience to their prelates* — not any indeed, nor those chosen by their own judgment, but *their own*, that is, those legitimately set over them by the Church: to obey them and follow them, *for they watch for our souls* (Heb 13:17), and just as *Paul* commends *Epaphras* to the *Colossians* as their ordinary pastor, and that they should receive him with grace and hold in honor, he prescribes (Phil 2:29). So specially he enjoins other churches also to honor their pastors and obey them, which certainly they would not do, if, neglecting these, they expected the work of others.

**(3)** *There is also the general rule of Apostle Paul*, that *all things in the Church should be done in order and decently* (1 Cor 14:40). Great confusion would arise if one, on light cause, should frequently change his pastor, and adhere sometimes to one, sometimes to another orthodox in the faith. If this permutation should happen on account of the *gifts of pastors*, which in others are more excellent — let them remember what the Apostle wrote to the Corinthians, when on account of diversity of gifts in his ministers they were making *schisms*, some joining themselves to Apollos, others to Peter, others to Paul: by which name he objected: *is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?* (1 Cor 1:5,6); *what is Paul, what is Apollo? But ministers, through whom ye believed, and to each God has given as he willed* (1 Cor 3:4,5). And if this permutation is from *hatred or wrath* toward the pastor, let the auditors consider *how great a sin they contaminate themselves with*. *Have peace with all men, if it be possible, and as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all* (Rom 12:18) — much more with your pastors. But if from these they separate themselves in wrathful mind, they add sin to sin — for with a mind implacable against their pastor, they seek their soul's care from a stranger, which is nothing else than to serve God in sins, and to contemn the counsel of Scripture, *about reconciliation with the neighbor before we approach sacred things* (Matt 5:23,24; Mark 11:25), and *about lifting up hands to God without wrath* (1 Tim 2:8).

**(4)** *Many damages also flow from this permutation.* The pastor who is deserted is rendered suspect, as though he administers not his office as befits the dignity — although in the matter itself injury may be done to him. Scandal is given to others, who by this example easily change their pastors also — whereby the reason of obedience owed to the ministry, together with all discipline, would easily collapse. *License to sin* is introduced: for while auditors wander from one pastor to another, no one has accurate care of them, and no one is bold to censure their vices freely, since it always must be feared that, this pastor being again deserted, they will seek another.

**(5)** *The ancients well considered this*, therefore orthodox fathers both in councils and in their private writings seriously disapproved this custom of permuting pastors. In the *III Council of Carthage* (at which *Augustine* was present), cap. 10 (whence there is a canon): *it pleased, that plebes of others not be usurped by any bishop, nor should any bishop trespass into the diocese of another his colleague*. *Cyprian* (lib. 1 ep. 6) writes: *without doubt they acquire the greatest perdition of themselves in indignation of God, who make schism, leaving their bishop, another false-bishop constituting for themselves*. And (lib. 1 ep. 3): *it has been established by us all, and it is equal and equally just, that the cause of each shall there be heard where the crime was committed; and to each pastor a portion of the flock has been ascribed, which each governs and rules, to give account of his action to the Lord. Those over whom we preside ought not to run about, nor by their subtle and fallacious temerity to collide the concord of bishops*. So in the *Canon Law* (lib. 5 *decretal.* Gregory tit. 39, which is *de parochiis*, c. *ut Dominicis*), from the *Nannetensian Council* it is sanctioned: *that on Lord's Days or feast days, the presbyters, before they celebrate mass, should interrogate the plebs, whether there be any parishioner in the Church who, contemning his own presbytery, should wish to hear mass there — whom, if he be found, they should straightway cast forth from the Church*. And (lib. 5 tit. 38, which is *de poenitentiis et remissionibus*), it is sanctioned in c. *omnis*, that *each one should confess to his own priest — but if anyone shall for a just cause wish to confess his sins to another priest, let him first ask license from his own priest, because otherwise he cannot absolve him or bind him*.

It stands from all these things, both from Scripture and from reason and confirmed in the primitive Church, *that each one should be content with his ordinary pastor in the care of the soul, and not use another's work, unless from most urgent necessity*.

### Case VI. What is to be done by those who dwell among enemies of God, from whom they are deprived of the ministers of their souls, and have no power to call others?

**Respondeo.** First of all, those who in their heart are convinced that hitherto they have received the pure Word of God from their pastors, and that the doctrine to which they are addicted is undoubtedly true, let them give thanks to God for the recognition of the truth, and stiffen their mind not to be moved a hair's breadth from it. For *they who retain the beginning of their substance firm to the end are truly participants of Christ* (Heb 3:14). Wherefore let them not induce their minds to hear false doctors, among whom they live *as sheep among wolves*. *My sheep hear my voice*, says Christ, *and they know me and follow me; but a stranger they do not follow, but flee from him* (John 10:27,5). Thus *Naaman the Syrian* dwelt in the midst of an idolatrous people, and even accompanied his king to the temple of Rimmon, since by reason of his office he could not omit — yet in that temple he did not worship the idols of the gentiles, but adored his God (2 Kgs 5:18). In the time of *Elijah* there were 7000 in the households who *did not bend the knee before Baal*, nor heard the Baalites, but *privately with their own persevered in the doctrine they had learned from their parents*, and exercised themselves in it. Therefore those who live *in the Papacy*, being deprived of orthodox doctors, ought not to mix themselves with the sacred rites of Romanists, but can hold exercises of piety with their own privately — always remembering that Apostolic admonition: *depart from her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins* (Rev 18:4) — and *be ye not unequally yoked with unbelievers* (2 Cor 6:14).

And although *per se* it is not prohibited to enter the temples of the adversaries, yet this is not useful to all — because not all are so confirmed in the faith, that without scandal they can be present at those *Papist* sacred rites; therefore here has place that of the Apostle *Paul* (1 Cor 6:12; 10:23): *all things are lawful for me, but not all things expedient*.

If any however by reason of office and ministry are compelled to attend with those whom they serve, let them imitate *Naaman*, and separate themselves in mind from that idolatrous worship — of which we treated at length above in Cap. 6, Case 6.

**Above all let the auditors beware, lest against the ordinary magistrate — who has expelled orthodox doctors — they machinate anything by external force, either by open or clandestine tumults; nor by words and revilings should they do him injury; nor should they liberate their doctors by arms from the hand of the persecutors. For these are not legitimate media of defending religion.**

Therefore holy men have always dehortated their own from these. *Eusebius Vercellensis* under the *Valentian Emperor*, punished with exile because of the faith, when his auditors would liberate him by force from prison, resisted their attempt — testifying that subjects ought to obey even an unjust magistrate, until God, by other legitimate means, granted Halcyonian days to his Church. *Ambrose*, when *Auxentius* prefect under the *Emperor Valens* held the *Apostle* imprisoned, and the auditors wished to liberate him from prison by armed hand, dehortated them, that they should not attempt anything against the magistracy of the *Emperor*.

*By other means therefore should this evil be met.* First of all, let them possess their souls in patience, *commending to God this injury which they cannot resist*. Let them consider that Christ predicted this event to his disciples: *when they persecute you in one city, flee ye into another* (Matt 10:23).

Then, *privately* let them treat with their own, recall to their memories and diligently to their studies the things which they earlier heard from the faithful pastors of their souls, praying for the safety of their pastors — just as the *seven thousand* in the time of the *Baalitic* persecution and the citizens of *Jerusalem*, when Herod persecuted the Apostles and had cast *Peter* into prison, meanwhile continuously prayed for him to God, who heard their prayers and sent unexpected help from heaven (Acts 12).

Third, *if the auditors observe that the enemies of the Gospel are not content with mere relegation of the doctors, but threaten them with death, they do not sin if they consult for their salvation* — just as *Paul's* disciples, when the prefect of *King Aretas* wished to arrest him, *let him down by a basket*, and thus preserved their master (Acts 9:25; 2 Cor 11:33). Also *Obadiah* hid a hundred Prophets in the time of the *Baalitic* persecution in caves (1 Kgs 18). For here has place that saying of Solomon: *he who takes away the innocent, when he is being led to death, and delivers him — is not this a witness of your good works?* (Prov 24:11,12).

Then also, *suppliant vows are to be poured out to God*, that the minds of the enemies may be mollified, that they may consent to the restitution of pastors and public exercises — in which class of *prayers and intercessions* often much profit is derived, provided all be done *modestly and prudently, from serious love toward the purity of the divine Word*, than which nothing is dearer to the pious. So *Samuel* prays for *Saul* cast off from the kingdom (1 Sam 15:11); *Ebedmelech* prays for *Jeremiah* thrown into the pit (Jer 38:9); *the prefect Sales*, when he observed the patience and constancy of Christians under the persecution of the Arian emperor, interceded for them, and mollified the emperor's wrath. Through the intercession of *Esther* the free exercise of religion was restored to the Jews (Esth 8). Similar examples occur everywhere in histories.

If not even by this reason anything be effected, there is need of patience and prayers to be poured out to God, who to his Church promised that not even the *gates of hell* should prevail against her; and he himself will send help to the oppressed. For not for perpetuity does he give affliction to the just (Ps 55:23) — as it is said in the proverb: *when the necessity is at its peak, God is nearest*.

*So much of the hearing of the divine Word. Now follow cases which concern the use of the sacraments — of which in this chapter we shall make a beginning from Baptism.*

— ❦ —

## Chapter XI. On Cases of Conscience Concerning the Use of the Sacraments, and Especially of Baptism

*De casibus conscientiae circa usum sacramentorum, et in specie baptismi.*

*Sacraments* are so called (as *Augustine* speaks, lib. 19 *contra Faustum* c. 16, and in *Levitico* q. 84) — *the words of visible and invisible grace, of visible signs*. For by these words is as it were subjoined that which by the *spoken Word* the auditor perceives — namely the promise of grace, and whatever is proposed to us in the Word to be believed concerning our salvation.

In this kind God accommodates himself to our weakness. For *when he saw in us corporeal creatures how we should be, he gave us divine grace also in a corporeal manner*, as *Chrysostom* speaks on Matthew (Hom. 82). *If thou wert incorporeal, he would have given thee incorporeal gifts; but since thou art conjoined to a body, in things sensible are the intelligibles delivered to thee*.

We presuppose here, as demonstrated elsewhere, that in the New Testament there are two sacraments: **Baptism** and the **Lord's Supper**. About the use of these fall not a few things which can render the conscience of man doubtful — in unfolding which our work shall now be occupied; in this chapter we shall make a beginning from Baptism.

### Case I. Is the use of the sacraments so necessary to salvation that no one can be saved without them?

**Respondeo.** Concerning this question the conscience is troubled in this part: (1) by those things which against the necessity of Baptism are disputed *by the Photinians* and *Calvinists*; and (2) by many cases which exclude a man from the use of the sacraments.

*The Photinians deny that Baptism is necessary to salvation*, because it is not instituted by Christ, nor was it enjoined to the disciples, but only permitted — because Christ so ordered it as the common convenience of the age required, as *Socinus* speaks (*De baptismo aquae* c. 2).

*The Calvinists* say that baptism is necessary indeed, but not as a *medium of regeneration*, but only *as a sign* by which the true Church of God is discerned from the false — partly as a *testimony of a man's incorporation into the Church*, as *Perkins* (*In casibus conscient.* lib. 1 c. 24 Quaest. 2 sect. 1) and *Trelcatius* (*Institut.* lib. 2 part. 2 *de baptismo* p. 194). They deny then that Baptism is a necessary organ through which faith, regeneration, and salvation are conferred. Hence *Calvin* himself writes (*Instit.* lib. 4 c. 15 § 20): *how much harm has this dogma brought in, which was ill exposed — that baptism is by the necessity of salvation — few observe*. For which cause the saying of Christ (John 3) *unless a man be born again of water and of the Spirit* they take improperly, as though by *water* he understood the *Holy Spirit* — which exposition is not altogether alien from *Bede* (in the *Response to the profession of faith of Monk Burdegal* art. 11 and *Perkins* in *Cas. consc.* loc. cit.). *Musculus* also (loc. commun. c. 28) reprehends those *who bring their infants to baptism as if to salvation, and if it is deferred longer, weep — with which sentence Nazianzen also agreed, that the baptism of infants may be deferred to the third year*: which places declare *that from that error, as if to salvation necessary, it is not attracted*.

Nor is the opposite opinion opposed by the Savior himself, who says we are born again *of water and Spirit* — not that the gift of the newly regenerating is sealed by water (John 3). To this the Apostle Paul, who testifies that *Christ cleansed the Church by the laver of water in the Word* (Eph 5:26), and calls baptism *the laver of regeneration and renovation in Christ* (Titus 3:5): by which words baptism must be not signal that seals but the seal effectively.

We should know therefore: **(I)** *that not by all things is the same the necessity of baptism and of the Holy Supper*. For by baptism we are inserted into Christ and into his mystical body, in which we are preserved and confirmed in that. As therefore of *ingrafting into Christ* the necessity is greater than of *confirmation* (for this all indeed indigate, who desire to be participants of Christ; that only the tempted and floating in faith), so the necessity of Baptism is greater than of the Holy Supper. For infants may lack the latter, but not the former.

**(II)** We should know that baptism is *not absolutely necessary* to salvation, so that no one who is not baptized can be saved; but only *from hypothesis* — namely, if a case of necessity does not obstruct. For outside the case of necessity, when God ordinarily works salvation in us, we cannot lack baptism: **(1)** because the precept of Christ is clear — *teach all nations, baptizing them* (Matt 28:19); and *he who has believed and been baptized shall be saved* (Mark 16). **(2)** *The words of Christ* to *Nicodemus* also are not obscure: *unless one is born again of water and of the Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven* (John 3) — where clearly *baptism* is treated as the ordinary medium of our regeneration, which Christ commends to Nicodemus, unless one wants to render his words vain. **(3)** *For all infants regeneration is necessary* (John 3:5); therefore also baptism, without which regeneration does not happen in the ordinary way. **(4)** *The necessity of baptism* even the *Apostles* and the *sons of Christ* acknowledged: for when the *Jews*, whose heart Peter had touched in his sermon, would ask what should be done that they might follow salvation, *Peter* responded: *let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ* (Acts 2:38); and when after his conversion Paul's sins were remitted by the Lord, *Ananias* said to him: *rise and be baptized, and wash away thy sins* (Acts 22:16).

**Now the error of the Calvinists arises** from this: that from baptism they exclude *sealing grace* — with which is inserted the fear of falling — but write that *Peter* declares in place: *baptism is the antitype of salvation*, as he speaks in the place cited. And they explain it *in place of a two-fold covenant*, that of the tables. And they oppose *the Savior himself*, who says we are born again *by water and Spirit* — not, as they hold, is the gift of one being newly regenerated sealed by water (John 3). Also the Apostle Paul, who testifies that *Christ cleansed the Church by the laver of water in the Word* (Eph 5:26), and calls baptism *the laver of regeneration and renewal in Christ* (Titus 3:5): by which words baptism must not signify something that only signal-seals but effectively-seal.

**And these things indeed so hold, when God ordinarily works in us.** But in the case of necessity God also *outside baptism gives faith, and confers salvation*. For God is free, who has bound us indeed to certain means which he shows in his Word, so that we cannot with piety negligence them and should be damnable — but he himself did not bind himself to those. Therefore Christ does not simply damn those who are not baptized, but those who *have not believed* (Mark 16:16).

*The case of necessity is*, when infants in the womb of the mother, or a little after birth, die, so that they cannot be baptized — although the parents wanted baptism most eagerly; or when adults at last in the final moment of life are converted, and are otherwise impeded from baptism, as *the thief on the cross* (Luke 23:43). There is no contempt of the sacrament; but only privation, which does not damn.

**(III)** *As for the Lord's Supper*, its use is not necessary for all, but only for those who have arrived at maturity of age, who can prove themselves (1 Cor 11:28). These can partake more frequently, because they need this spiritual aliment continually to renew the spiritual life in the faithful: therefore in the words of institution is added, *do this, as often as ye do it, in remembrance of me*.

Yet not *absolutely* necessary is the use of the Holy Supper — but with urgent necessity, with salvation and conscience preserved, it may be omitted. Urgent necessity is when we have a serious desire for this salutary aliment, but we cannot obtain it — whether on account of contagious disease, or on account of pilgrimages undertaken for just causes, or on account of captivity among barbarians, or for some other case excluded from sacred assemblies. In these cases also is *no contempt, but privation* of the transiting sacrament — therefore *Augustine's* saying finds place: *believe, and thou hast eaten*.

But those who *without just cause* subtract themselves from the use of this sacrament, are contemners, and deprive themselves of its salutary fruit at great peril, nor are they worthy to be admitted either to the reception of infants at baptism or to the communion of other sacred things.

### Case II. Whence is faith conferred [in baptism upon infants]? And how is it conferred?

**Respondeo.** The matter is in itself sufficiently certain, against the *Anabaptists*, who do not admit infants before the years of discretion to baptism, because they think that defect of reason obstructs, that they cannot believe.

**(1)** The *Calvinists* also are refuted, who deny to infants an *actual faith*, but only a habit, an inchoation and as it were a seed and root, as *Gregor. de Valentia* speaks (*De baptismo parvulorum* c. 3), *Beza* (part. 2 resp. ad Acta Trelc. lib. 2 *institut.*). *The Calvinist Grosius* [Grosseteste?], who make baptism only a sign of the covenant, than as an organ through which faith is conferred, as *Perkins* in the place above cited satisfies, and teach that parents apprehend the covenant both for themselves and for their children, and that the children believe because parents believe.

Whoever without just cause subtract themselves from the use of this sacrament are contemners.

**Adjoined to these in reason, though not in name, are those who leave their children without baptism** for often frivolous causes — not only for days, but even for several weeks. If they knew with how great peril of salvation infants would be neglected by themselves, without doubt they would be more cautious in this kind.

Since therefore without faith no salvation is to be hoped, it is worth the effort to teach the following by arguments — that in *infants*, through Baptism as an ordinary organ of God, faith is conferred:

**(1) *Reason 1.*** It is certain that infants also of pious parents are, outside baptism, even outside grace, since they *are born and conceived in sins*, as David complains (Ps 51:5); *of the flesh they are born as flesh* (John 3:6); *by nature they are sons of wrath* (Eph 2:3), that is, sons of anger. Therefore outside baptism they are under wrath, not under grace. But in baptism they are received into grace and please God, because *baptism is the entrance into the Church*, through which they enter and become members and domestics of God. Therefore those who from Judaism or Gentilism are converted to Christ, are baptized (Acts 2:38; 8:38; 10:48; 12:15). Now without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb 11:6); whence it follows that infants, who in baptism begin to please God, receive faith while they are baptized.

**(2) *Reason 2.*** *To infants belongs the kingdom of heaven* (Mark 10:14; Matt 19:14), which that they may enter, they need baptism: *unless one is born again of water and Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven* (John 3:5). But to the kingdom of heaven no one has access who does not believe: for *he who does not believe shall be damned* (Mark 16:16). Hence again most firmly we gather that in infants faith is conferred in baptism.

**(3) *Reason 3.*** *Baptism is the laver of regeneration* (Titus 3:5), through which we are made *sons of God* — which without faith does not happen; for *God gave power to become sons of God to those who believe in his name* (John 1:12). And by this very thing *regeneration is discerned from natural generation*, that this indeed [natural generation] is of the unfaithful or of sons of wrath, that indeed [regeneration] of the faithful: therefore *born again should Christians become*, says *Tertullian* (Apolog. c. 16): *Christians are not born but made from Christians, because it is not generation, but regeneration*, says *Augustine* (lib. 1 *de peccat. merit.* c. 8).

**(4) *Reason 4.*** *The Apostle Paul says* (Gal 3:27) *we in baptism have put on Christ*. Now *to put on Christ* is to put on the *righteousness of Christ*, which righteousness elsewhere is called *the garment of salvation* (Isa 61:10). This is done through faith, which apprehends the righteousness of Christ, not our own.

**(5) *Reason 5.*** *The infants of the Hebrews were received into the covenant of God through the sacrament of circumcision* (Gen 17:10). Therefore those who were not circumcised were excluded from the people of God. The same is the ratio of baptism, which entered in place of circumcision. Therefore also baptism is called *the stipulation of a good conscience with God* (1 Pet 3:21), since it makes the man a certain participant of the divine covenant.

**(6) *Reason 6.*** *The Holy Spirit is not idle in the baptized*: his proper operation is in those who first accede to the Church, that he kindles in them faith, which after new motions of charity in adult age follow. Unless therefore we would deny to the baptized infants the Holy Spirit, or feign the Holy Spirit in them to be idle, we must confess that in baptism they receive faith. Hence is that of *Augustine* (Ep. 57): *the Holy Spirit is said to dwell in infants, because he in them occultly works, that they be his temples, which afterward through profession he perfects, and by profiting persevering*.

**(7) *Reason 7.*** Those who are not baptized when they can be baptized, are certainly damned — those who contemn that ordinary medium of their salvation. Therefore *a contrario sensu* I rightly gather, those who are baptized are saved, and consequently receive faith, without which no salvation is conferred. This attests *Augustine* (*Ad Fratrem Diaconum* c. 40): *most firmly hold, thou saidst, and doubt not in any way, except those who for the name of CHRIST are baptized in their own blood, no man shall accept eternal life who has not here been converted through penitence and faith, and by the sacrament of faith and of penitence — that is, by baptism — has been liberated; and for greater ones indeed be necessary through penitence to bear their evils and faith Catholic according to the rule of truth to hold, and to receive the sacraments of baptism; but for little ones, who neither by their own will can believe, nor perform penitence for the sin which originally they draw, the sacrament of faith, which is holy baptism, so long as the age of reason cannot be capable, suffices for salvation*.

Here accedes the testimony of *Ambrose*, who denies eternal life outright to the non-baptized: therefore he concedes faith to the baptized, without which no one can enter life. Thus he writes (lib. 1 *De vocatione gentium* c. 8): *nor is it right to believe, that those who have not obtained the sacrament of regeneration should pertain to any consortium of the blessed*. And (lib. *De Eliae jejunio* c. 22): *if anyone has not been baptized, more securely let him be converted, and receive remission of sins, since baptism as it were consumes sins by fire, because Christ baptizes in fire and spirit*.

Since therefore *Holy Spirit, faith, regeneration, salvation, baptism* are conjoined with an indivisible nexus, whoever understands, sees how ill they consult for their infants who defer their baptism without cause. **For if any think** that infants before baptism are in the covenant, and believe by the faith of the parents, these greatly err. For without Scripture they think this — which puts all not yet baptized, whom nature makes sons of wrath, outside the covenant. But conversely, *baptism is called the stipulation of ours with God* (1 Pet 3), and just as no one lives natural life by the soul of his parents, so no one can live before God by the faith of parents: but *the just shall live by his own faith* (Hab 2:4). For parents generate not in that part by which they are spirits and reborn, but in that part by which they are flesh and polluted: not otherwise than as a Jew circumcised without foreskin generates a son with foreskin, and bare grains put in the field generate grains with husks, ears of grain, awns, and chaff — with which similitudes *Augustine* uses in c. 10 *De peccati.* c. 2.

*Reponens ad exemp. Abrahae:* — Now it is objected: *God said to Abraham* (Gen 17): *I shall be thy God and of thy seed after thee*. But this is not to be understood without the determination of proper faith: for the *believers only* pertain to the seed of Abraham, as it is written (Gal 3:7): *those who are of faith, these are the sons of Abraham*. But God offers benefits to all men, though he confers only to those who through the medium instituted by him are rendered capable of perceiving those benefits.

But of these enough. From which it is sufficiently abundantly established, how *perilous* it is to defer the baptism of infants. *Moses* the Lord had wanted at least once to intercept, because he had deferred somewhat longer the circumcision of his infant (Exod 4:25); let those who procrastinate baptism see, lest they too incur God's animadversion for the unhappiness of their infants.

### Case III. What if an infant, before baptism, dies through the days of the parents' waiting?

**Respondeo.** In the *Papacy* there are four diverse opinions concerning this matter, all too rigid for the miserable infants and the afflicted parents, which we shall recount.

**(1) The first is of *Abraham Catharinus* and other rigorists, who *exclude infants dying in the womb, or immediately after birth, from the kingdom of heaven altogether*, but concede to them *natural blessedness* not molested by any pain, outside the kingdom of the blessed, and far from the prison of the damned — that is, in a middle place between heaven and hell.**

**(2) The second is of *Bellarmine*, *Bonaventure*, *Aquinas*, and other scholastics, who teach that infants of this kind are punished in the *limbo of children* (as they call it), but only with the *pain of loss* (*poena damni*), not of sense — that is, deprived of the vision and glory of God, but afflicted with no cruciate of the senses.**

**(3) The third is of *Lombard* and others, who think that such infants are freed from *hellfire*, but yet suffer some pain of loss, which follows the felicity of the blessed.**

**(4) The fourth is of *Gregory of Rimini*, *Thomas Bradwardine*, *Robert Holcot*, and other scholastic Realists, who make such infants heirs of eternal damnation, punished with both kinds of pain, both of loss and of sense, but not equally cruciated with adults.** *Bellarmine* (c. 21 *de bapt.*) partly indeed determines the little ones without baptism dying to be damned with pain of eternal damnation, yet not to feel *sensible fire*, but inner pain, because they understand themselves to be deprived of blessedness.

Innocent III also (in the chapter *Firmiter*) sets forth the *Catholic faith*, that infants who die without baptism are *not saved*: whence is the custom in the Papacy of privating non-baptized infants of the usual rite of burial, and burying them in a corner of the cemetery.

**And truly it cannot be denied**, that even *Augustine* once did not wish to inscribe non-baptized infants in the number of the saved (Ep. 28 and 108, and lib. *De nat. et grat.* c. 8, *De fide ad Petrum* c. 27). *For which reason with these pious parents are perpetually racked with anguish; but Augustine in other places speaks doubtfully of this matter* (lib. 1 *De peccat. merit. et remiss.* c. 15; lib. 3 *De origine animae* c. 18). Elsewhere he also *attributes faith to others who beyond their fault could not be baptized* (lib. 4 *De bapt. cont. Donatist.* c. 11; lib. 3 *quaest. in Levit.*).

**Milder Papists also contradict this rigid doctrine.** For when *Lombard* wrote in the place cited that little ones dying before baptism perish, the *Faculty of Paris* subscribed: *this is manifestly not held*. And in species *Joannes* Chancellor of the University of Paris, in the Sermon *De nativit. beatae Mariae Virginis*, sets it down: *God has not so bound the mercy of salvation to sacraments, that without prejudice of the same law he cannot within the womb, before they are yet born, sanctify little ones by his grace of baptism, or by the virtue of the Holy Spirit; therefore if parents pray to the Lord for the infant not yet born, which perhaps will die before it is baptized, he admonishes, and consoles them that if any without baptism thus depart, they should not despair of every hope of salvation*. Similar things are held by other Papists: *Gabriel Biel* (in 4. sent. dist. 4 quaest. 2 art. 3), *Cajetan* (in p. 3 Thom. ad quaest. 68 art. 11), *Albertus Pighius* (in *Controversia* 1).

**We however must observe the *fountains of consolation* by which pious parents in such cases can erect themselves.** *Gravely they erred of old*, who to infants in the womb of the mother periling of life used to sprinkle the mother's womb with water, and by this reason believed those infants to be baptized — which error *Augustine* refutes (lib. 6 *Contra Julianum Pelagianum* c. 5). And *Jerome* said: *from the maternal womb no one can be baptized, though the mother be baptized*. Not less err those who *in peril of life dip in water either the hand or the foot of the infant*; for not yet born he cannot be born again — therefore *Luther* reproved this custom (Tom. 5 *Jenens.* in the book *De abortientibus mulieribus*). And *Augustine* (Ep. 57 ad Dardanum): *there is here no consolation for afflicted parents; other fountains of consolation must be sought*.

**First then, most firmly must be held**, that *the promise made to Abraham* (Gen 17): *I shall be thy God and of thy seed after thee*, also pertains to us, though we are not of the very seed of Abraham. For *the gentiles are ingrafted by the grace of God into the olive, and are companions of the root and of the fatness of the olive* (Rom 11:17). Hence *the sons of Abraham are called believers* (Gal 3:7); to us also is *the promise made, and to your children, and to all who are far off* (Acts 2:39). *Without faith* however no one is a son of Abraham nor a participant of the olive: whence it follows that infants of Christians who cannot be baptized in the case of necessity are to hold themselves for *seed of Abraham*, to whom the promise is made — therefore of these God will have care, that they perish not, if they be deprived of the ordinary medium of salvation. For who shall prescribe to God the manner and mode of aiding our salvation?

**Then Christian parents know**, that their children *are the work of God's hands*, as *David* says (Ps 138:8): *the works of thy hands, O Lord, forsake not*. Whom just as *Job* in his straits sought consolation from this work of God, whose hands had fashioned him, and from whose hands he hoped for guardianship and protection (Job 10:8) — so pious parents ought firmly to confide, that God will not cast forth their children as his peculiar work and gift from before his face, even if beyond every fault of theirs they are compelled to lack baptism as an ordinary medium of regeneration.

**Moreover**, since outside Christ there is no salvation, pious parents can be certain that infants of theirs prevented by death are yet not outside Christ, even though through baptism they themselves could not be inserted. For *Christ is the Savior of infants*: therefore he was made *partaker of flesh and blood, as we are* (Heb 2:14); in the womb of his mother was he conceived, and from the flesh of his mother was he born as a boy — therefore also *of infants in the womb of the mother yet resting he is the redeemer*, whose polluted nativity by his immaculate nativity he sanctified. On which matter *Anselm* speaks preclarely: *he came to save all through himself, he came through every age of ours, and among infants he was made an infant, sanctifying infants* (Cur Deus Homo lib. 2 c. 26). And *Bernard* (Serm. 1 *In ramis palmarum*): *he who was a little one born, and first fought the array of the little ones, today no less excludes the little ones from grace, since neither is it uncongruous to piety nor difficult to his majesty, if by the supplement of grace he brings whatever nature does not yet permit as possible*.

[*Augustine* has also that memorable saying (Serm. 5 *De nativitate*): *to all of us this joyful message pertains, since Christ came for all; nor should any be excluded, especially in the place where the fountains of joys are opened. Let the saint rejoice, since he receives remuneration; let the sinner rejoice, since he is invited to pardon; let the gentile rejoice, since he is sent to life. Exult, holy children, since a boy is born; exult, virgins, since a virgin has borne; exult, sanctified ones, since he is your justifier; exult, weak and sick, since a savior is born; exult, captives, since a redeemer is born; exult, servants, since a Lord is born; exult, freemen, since a Liberator is born; exult, all Christians, since it is the birth of CHRIST.*]

Thus he is said to *bear the sins of the whole world*, and is called *Savior of the whole world*: from the world however infants are not excluded. And although through the ordinary means of consequent faith (through which the Savior of the world is apprehended) they are destitute, yet God does not lack faith, whom he knows extraordinarily to work in them — as we have shown above by given examples.

**Here fourthly pertains the examples**, of which the Scripture testifies, that *in the womb of the mother they were donated by the grace of God*. *David* certainly testifies (Ps 51:5) *he was conceived in sins*, yet confesses (Ps 22:10) *from the womb of the mother thou art my God*, and (Ps 139:13): *thou hast possessed my reins, thou hast received me from the womb of my mother*, &c. To *Jeremiah* says the Lord: *before I formed thee in the womb, I knew thee, and before thou wast born out of the womb, I sanctified thee* (Jer 1:5). Such projection into God, and sanctification, cannot be without faith. These examples do not show what ordinarily God does in all, yet teach *what he can and is wont to do*, even without ordinary means, since he is a most free agent, and does not so bind himself to certain means, that in the case of necessity, in defect of those means, he cannot otherwise operate.

**Fifthly**, examples are not lacking in *terms terminating*, as they say — namely of those who, before they had obtained the sacrament of initiation, yet had a good hope of their salvation. Among these were all those infants and adults in the primitive Church who, before they received baptism, were made *martyrs*, and to damn all these were of extreme temerity. Let pious parents cogitate therefore, that their infant also is *seed of Abraham* to whom the promise is made — therefore God will have care of him, that he perish not, deprived at most of the ordinary medium of salvation. For God has attached to himself in no place the grace of God to his glory: and where two or three are gathered in the name of Christ, there is the Church, and in its midst is CHRIST (Matt 18:20).

*All those infants and adults deprived* — the *Israelites among the murmurers*, who by God's command have not received his temple, and the flesh of no one damns them; those *Hebrew males*, who by Pharaoh's command as soon as born were exposed to death (Exod 1); *the infant Israelites*, who in the time of *Antiochus* the killer perished on the sabbath (1 Macc 1); *the infants of Bethlehem*, that first flower of NT martyrs, who by Herod's command were extinguished (Matt 2:16) — all these to make heirs of damnation, or at least excluded from the sight and glory of God, would be of great tyranny and impiety. Hither refers to certain, the infant that David begot from adultery, who on the seventh day (which we understand of the seventh from birth), died — before he could according to the law be circumcised (2 Sam 12). Yet the parent does not doubt that he is saved, when he says (v. 23): *I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me* — that is, he hopes to see him in that other blessed world. Some also consider that if he could have been suddenly cured, before he was baptized by his father's care, when Job says: *he sleeps and rests in slumber* — as of the blessed is described (Job 3:13). Since therefore in place of circumcision baptism succeeded, the same can be the consolation of pious parents whose infants by celerity of time are defrauded of baptism, not by the will of the parents.

**Finally**, that God not only *has been able*, but also *has willed* in infants in the case of necessity to work faith and regeneration, from the following arguments it is established:

**(1)** That to those indeed who have been baptized and believe, salvation is attributed, and when of the damned it must be said, no mention is made of the non-baptized, but of the unbelievers, as in Mark 16:16: *he who has not believed shall be damned*.

**(2)** God does not will that anyone perish, but wills that all be saved (2 Pet 3:9). *God wills all men to be saved* (1 Tim 2:4); and *of infants his will is that we not have contempt* (Matt 18:14). Since however those who do not believe must necessarily perish, it must not be doubted, that to them extraordinarily he bestows faith.

**(3)** For certain are the promises of God concerning the hearing of prayers, especially those which by two or three conjoined in Christ's name are made (Matt 18:19,20,22).

Since therefore an infant is still borne in the womb, let the parents acknowledge the *gift of God*, by which they have blessed him with their marriage, giving thanks that he has dignified them with the illustrious honor of *fathers* and *mothers*, let them avoid all external things by which some detriment can be inflicted on the infants in the womb: above all, however, with ardent prayers let them invoke God, that he himself may have care of the work of his own hands, guarding the infant in the womb, and on account of his most beloved Son the *Infant*, cleanse him from sins in which he was conceived, and receive him into the *covenant of grace*, and effectuate the *end of life eternal*, for which he was created.

**These prayers God will not permit to be idle**: for he himself mandated them, and he promised the hearing (Ps 50:15; Ps 65:3; Matt 18:19; John 16:23). Whence we have already heard, that *the Sacrament of Baptism is chief of those things by which infants are offered to the Lord*. Wherefore, when a father *dies* by *celerity of the time was prevented*, that he does not lose salvation by his faith — from which two-fold testimony of the fathers *Bernard* speaks (Ep. 77): *he plainly and evidently shows* (Saint Augustine) *that the faithful and one converted to the Lord, if he cannot but has contemned baptism, and cannot be deprived of baptism — hitherto he leans on two columns* (I speak of Augustine and Ambrose): *believe me, difficult it is that thou lookest back. With these, I say, either to err or to know I confess, believing myself, faith alone can save a man, when the desire to receive the sacrament: if however anticipating pious desire, or any other invincible thing obviated, see also, lest by chance on this account it be saved. For when he said, "he who has believed and been baptized, shall be saved," so cautiously and vigilantly he did not repeat: "he who has not been baptized" — but only "he who has not believed," he says, "shall be damned" — namely, indicating faith alone sometimes to suffice for salvation, but without it to suffice nothing*. In the same epistle *Bernard* writes: *the profitable will is imputed, where the fact is excluded by necessity*.

All these things, for tranquilizing the conscience of pious parents who by this case of their children are consternated, can suffice.

### Case IV. Concerning those who in the Papacy were baptized with other rites than those used among the orthodox, and though baptized in the Papist faith, are yet in adult age not addicted to that religion — if they later are anguished on this name, whether concerning their baptism they should doubt or not

**Respondeo.** When we treat of the truth of baptism, we should always distinguish its *substance* from its *ceremonies*. The substance is recognized from the words of institution — namely, that he be baptized in water in the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Ceremonies are either taken from the Apostles themselves, or added post-Apostolically in time. Those [Apostolic] the *Damascene* calls *Apostolic ecclesiastical ceremonies*. Apostolic are the prayers, thanksgivings, actions, and exhortations to the people: that of this kind ceremonies were used by the Apostles, is established from Acts 2:38 seqq.
